Cavity magnomechanics offers an excellent platform for investigating macroscopic quantum phenomena by coupling magnons within an external electromechanical environment. Identifying abnormal activities within video surveillance remains a vital component in ensuring public safety, a task complicated by the unpredictable and chaotic nature of crowd movements. Recent years have seen neural architecture search (NAS) emerge as a essential phase within the machine learning pipeline, significantly enhancing performance for numerous tasks, specifically within deep learning. While standard methods like random and grid searches have proven inadequate for this purpose due to excessively high computational costs, various approaches utilizing reinforcement learning, evolutionary strategies, variational methods alongside guidance from human expertise have gained prominence. Although these techniques offer progress, most fail to generalize effectively when confronted with altered properties in workloads or inference environments such as hardware constraints. To resolve this issue, we introduce a search strategy guided by properties that has a distinct advantage when properties are modified: we propose a novel method that utilizes the available property-data-in-out (DIO) relationship to guide the search process, effectively constructing a probabilistic model representing the design space through representation that maps structural patterns and their corresponding effects on the properties. Our experiments, which compare against state-of-the-art techniques, demonstrate our model's superior capability in searching for effective neural architectures that meet specific structural requirements, notably reducing computational costs by approximately 90%.

Multicast beamforming is an effective strategy for delivering diverse content efficiently, yet creating independent precoders every time adds significant computational overhead. Benefiting from spatial diversity in millimeter-wave (mmWave) systems, sparse channel characteristics allow us to reduce this overhead through pilot-based methods like hybrid zero-forcing. However, because mmWave channels are rarely orthogonal, these traditional pilot-based approaches are generally unsuitable for addressing non-orthogonal multigroup scenarios. To counter this, we introduce a new technique called HGZFT (Hybrid Generalized Zero-Forcing Transceiver), designed specifically for optimizing multigroup multicast transmission using minimal multiantenna hardware. Our framework constructs a low-complexity hardware-efficient model by approximating fractional power constraints with a manageable bound that ensures rapid convergence via an alternating optimization methodology. Furthermore, by leveraging quasi-orthogonal channel properties found in multigroup wireless environments, we propose simplified configurations based on hybrid generalized zero forcing. Finally, simulation results validate that the proposed HGZFT method outperforms existing baseline algorithms in both beamforming gains and computational efficiency.

Communication bottlenecks remain a persistent obstacle within the federated learning framework. To address this, we introduce a novel strategy termed communication-efficient federated distillation (CED), which modifies both the communication architecture for knowledge transfer and the learning process itself. In the communication phase, the cloud distills distilled knowledge from model updates submitted by clients, effectively compressing information while enabling these updates to function as inputs for knowledge transfer rather than standard training data. On the training side, the cloud updates its global model by utilizing this distilled knowledge, operating exclusively on knowledge received, which reduces the data volume required for aggregation significantly. Furthermore, the system enables joint distilled knowledge transfer and facilitates efficient aggregation by aggregating knowledge transfer instead of the full model updates from all clients. Simulation results demonstrate savings in communication efficiency, showing that the proposed method can reduce update transmission from clients by as much as 92%, while maintaining global model accuracy that rivals standard feder learning despite utilizing data from only a subset of communicating clients.

In future networking paradigms such as Information-Centric Networking (ICN) and Network Function Virtualization (NFV), users will access information alongside embedded computation capabilities. NDN-based computing models enable this access, offering designs that allow requesters to perform calculations in the most suitable functionally equipped nodes. However, because moving data and computing tasks between sites incurs expenses, determining the optimal strategy to execute computations is essential for minimizing total costs. This research introduces ODCO (Optimal Dynamic Computing Orchestration), a mechanism designed to reduce movement expenses while executing requests triggered by users. Furthermore, to validate its efficacy and efficiency, ODCO has been implemented within the Mininet simulation environment and benchmarked against two existing base algorithms. Results demonstrate ODCO's superiority in lowering costs compared to these traditional methods.

This research investigates the stability of a specific Euler-Pernour beam model connected across a star-shaped network. By applying appropriate boundary conditions and utilizing Laplace transform techniques alongside specific kernel equations, we determine that exponential stability arises from suitable boundary control strategies. This study examines whether inhomogeneous chiral phases exist within the quark-meson model, which incorporates explicit chiral-symmetry breaking. Results indicate that although the region permitting these inhomogeneities diminishes as pion mass increases, such phases persist at the physical pion mass. Furthermore, instability driving inhomogeneous matter formation manifests in the scalar channel, as opposed to the less favorable pseudoscalar modes.

Utilizing both density functional theory (DFT) and $\Delta$-self-consistent junction gap DFT ($\Delta$SCF), we analyzed the electronic structures and stability of $M{Tl}_4{Te}_3$ ($M = \text{Cd, Hg}$) compounds. These materials exhibit $2e^-$-per formula unit surface states characteristic of topological insulators (TIs) and possess type-$2$ Dirac cones near the Fermi level. The analysis suggests that $M{Tl}_4{Te}_3$ forms an antiferromagnetic topological insulator with an extremely large band gap when exposed to air. Furthermore, we demonstrated that $M{Tl}_4{Te}_3$ is more stable than $M{Tl}_4{Se}_3$ ($M = \text{Cd, Hg}$) and $M{Tl}_4$I$_3$ ($M = \text{Hg, Cd}$) by evaluating their formation energies.

Current multi-objective optimization approaches rely on utility functions to guide the search, yet the necessary weights for these functions are often difficult to determine ahead of time. Therefore, we present an effective method for automatically learning these utility weights during the search process by integrating gradient descent to maximize a predetermined baseline utility function drawn from previous human optimization efforts of similar problems. By incorporating the calculated gradients of this reference utility, we can then construct a final weighted aggregate utility function that integrates crucial gradient information from multiple sources, including the reference function, past successful optimizations, and domain expert knowledge. Experimental validation across four benchmarks with varying levels of expert involvement demonstrates that our proposed approach consistently outperforms baseline optimization strategies that utilize time-proportionally balanced weights.

Recent investigations have indicated that agents trained via reinforcement learning (RL) are susceptible to adversarially crafted perturbations. Our research advances this field by demonstrating that minimal data can achieve significant the suppression of RL agents' performance when that data incorporates approximate temporal relationships. Specifically, our approach utilizes short trajectories to construct an attack model utilizing basic short-term recall mechanisms, such as n-grams or Permutation Mutual Maxing Encoding (PMME), which dynamically anticipate upcoming states or actions. While the utilization of short trajectory fragments is typical in state-of-the-art state-attack methodologies (MARL), such as shortest path, we are the first to highlight that these segments retain sufficient information when augmented with time dimensions to substantially compromise other types of state-attack models, including those using shortest path, as shown previously by others when applied to state-ordered inputs.

Organizations utilize issue tracking systems (ITS) to manage business tasks ranging from minor corrections to major feature developments. While system usage is a key management tool, a critical challenge remains the limited availability of datasets, which hinders the extensive development and deployment of automated services designed to assist with IT management. Existing public datasets are a subset of Jira repositories but are outdated and insufficient for effective research. This study introduces a new dataset compiled by downloading and merging over 300 public Jira repositories, resulting in approximately 1.1 million issues, 4 million comments, and 35 million character strings. We analyze the dataset's statistical characteristics and demonstrate its utility by developing four models—issue detection, comment issue sentiment classification, user language style imitation, and repository identification—while making these resources open for the community.

Distributed machine learning (DML) represents a pivotal technique for scaling large-scale learning tasks across distributed computational environments, enabling scenarios such as cross organization collaborations or the utilization of cloud infrastructure. In DML, each node accesses a subset of the total training data and individually trains a specialized aggregation function to combine localized knowledge into a unified global model. While Hsieh et al. originally proposed optimal aggregation functions within the linear framework that minimize empirical risk by accounting for data distribution and individual models, this linearity constraint frequently proves inadequate for complex, high-complexity problems.

This research presents the derivation of novel optimal aggregation functions belonging to a new non-linear family. Combani analysis reveals that these optimal functions retain significant properties useful for optimization and statistical interpretation. Furthermore, empirical evaluations across various benchmark DML scenarios demonstrate that the proposed methods substantially outperform traditional linear baselines, leading to higher performance with fewer nodes or markedly fewer training iterations.

Offering meaningful privacy protection for users of location-based systems presents considerable challenge, particularly when we consider that multiple visits by one individual to the same or nearby places frequently lead to the complete identification of their home and workplace. Recent efforts to achieve this have largely concentrated on obscuring specific locations through the release of vague geometrics—such as generalized zones or polygons—or by employing correlated synthetic datasets. In contrast, this paper introduces a distinct approach that utilizes the conditional probabilities of visit patterns to mask an individual's precise whereabouts. We have developed a novel algorithm capable of generating this probabilistically informed masking, and the paper includes a rigorous mathematical proof alongside an extensive empirical demonstration showing the method's significant effectiveness in preserving privacy.

Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) facilitates functional connectivity investigations without the need for task execution. Although widely utilized in clinical settings to detect deviations from normal connectivity patterns, rs-fMRI remains limited by slow image acquisition resulting in insufficient statistical power. This limitation frequently necessitates the combination of data from multiple centers to enhance robustness. However, such heterogeneous collections introduce site-specific biases due to discrepancies in scanners or protocols. Current solutions address this by incorporating site-correcting algorithms during analysis, yet their ability to mitigate location effects while preserving biologically meaningful signals is uncertain. This study evaluates the performance of various methods in maintaining signal retention and statistical reliability when using multiple sites. Using realistic simulations based on task-based fMRI data, we represent multiple locations with distinct functional structures and overlay them with multiple locations' worth of confounding offset constants alongside various noise conditions. We test three different strategies to handle the heterogeneous locations including no adjustment, harmonic regression of the offset, and ComPro correction. Results indicate that while harmonic regression successfully removes the offset variations, it fails to discard some noise sources. Conversely both ComPro and ComPro offset correction can remove the offset variations as well as reduce noise. We suggest that ComPro and ComPro offset correction methods balance statistical reliability and accuracy better than harmonic regression when using multiple locations to enhance statistical power.

While Federated Learning (FL) excels at cross-device model sharing, it struggles with Federated Semi-Supervised Learning (FSSL) due to the Disagreement Problem caused by heterogeneous local data distributions among clients. Specifically, when labeled data is scarce and data splits are non-IID, distinguishing between overfitted bad modes and globally optimal good modes becomes difficult. To address this, we introduce a new update mechanism termed Uncertainty Minimization (UM). Unlike global data distribution statistics that local clients cannot verify, UM focuses on minimizing uncertainty within each client's support set. By analyzing both data-driven and network-driven sources of uncertainty locally and within packets transmitted to the server, we establish a theoretical framework proving that our proposed UM method ensures convergence. Empirical evaluations on real-world benchmarks using synthetic BERT networks and VITs demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing methods.

Black-hole-neutron-star (BH-NS) merger magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) simulations are crucial for interpreting gravitational-wave signals and guiding future observatory searches. Nevertheless, these simulations remain computationally demanding, especially when accurately modeling thermal effects and neutrino radiative transfer. Conversely, unradiative non-thermal MHD approaches are more efficient but fail to capture neutron degeneracy pressure and heating, which are vital for precise simulations of prolonged (seconds-long) mergers and subsequent hypermassive neutron-star (HMNS) remnants. To address this gap, we present novel general-relativistic neutrino-MHD (NMHD) simulations of BH-NS mergers that incorporate neutrino opacities and thermal equilibrium between quanta and fermions. Our analysis covers a range of initial neutron-star mass deformations and explores different equations of state, while also calculating post-merger neutrino-luminosity spectra. These findings reveal that (i) high opacities facilitate an efficient magnetohydrodynamic dynamo within the HMNS, yielding a strong magnetic field aligned with the neutron-star rotational axis; (ii) in highly opaque regimes, magnetic-field orientation and post-merger evolution are primarily dictated by neutrino opacities and thermal dynamics, secondary to specific initial conditions.

The primary goal of this note is to determine the rate at which a conditioned process approximates a specific Q-process, based on appropriate properties of the process's quasi-stationary distribution. In contrast, we also demonstrate that when a conditioned process exhibits uniform convergence to both a conservative and ergodic Markov process, its associated Q-process is ultimately ergodic and exhibits power decay in its Poisson kernel. As a further application, we illustrate how these findings apply to a representing process derived from an ergodic environment where observations are subject to censoring.

This research introduces a novel strategy for assembling nanoparticles arranged in a hexagonal configuration within the optical near-field of a graphene sheet. Rooted in the strong light-matter interaction characteristic of graphene, this method leverages surface plasmon excitations to create a position-dependent optical binding mechanism governed by alterations in near-field energy. Consequently, controlling nanoparticle positioning becomes possible through tunable optical parameters, specifically intensity and frequency of incident light, as well as chemical doping levels. Furthermore, we examine an alternative arrangement where nanoparticles form a linear chain; in this scenario, orientation-dependent interactions emerge as a direct result of graphene's anisotropic conductance. Finally, potential applications of this approach for creating functional nanodevices are explored.

This study analyzes treatment time averages within the Emergency Department as functions of EKG-based risk levels for arrhythmias detecting rare conditions like this using specialized methods for accurate analysis. By applying these techniques, we derive smooth curves that remain reliable across all stages, allowing comparison among different patient categories. Findings indicate that, generally, higher-risk categories exhibit longer average treatment durations; however, at the very highest risk level in one specific category observed, a shorter average average time occurred. We conclude that using average response time alongside risk-based smoothing yields consistent and smooth curves capable of comparison across various patient types. If necessary further adjustments or analysis adjustments can ensure data integrity and meaningful comparisons between emergency scenarios.

We introduce and examine a distributed communication network structure designed for heterogeneous agent-based systems, where each node connects neighbors within a communication radius $R$. This regular and deterministic topology enables neighbors to interact directly. Our primary focus lies in determining the optimal value of $R$ to optimize performance, taking into account various robustness requirements. To address this problem, we first establish an information-theoretic performance bound, which reveals a fundamental limitation in communication regular topologies that forces local interactions, thereby restricting global information access. Consequently, this limitation results in inter-task correlations within task distributions across different agents. Leveraging this derived correlation structure, we present a computationally efficient algorithm for estimating an optimal $R$. This method relies solely on communication channel characteristics and local computations by individual nodes, requiring no knowledge of the total node count within the network. Simulations further illustrate the performance of our proposed algorithm.

The surge in online fundraising platforms has prompted businesses to seek better methods for predicting project success, as current online systems offer limited insights into which initiatives are likely to receive funding. Crowds within these platforms often generate observable signals—such as textual, visual, and audible interactions—and this study examines how group behavior correlates with funding outcomes across three specific platforms. Utilizing platforms Indiegogo, Kickstarter, and GoFundMe, which vary in the allowed media (text only, video, or video/audible), this research applies advanced machine learning techniques to analyze both media types from over 1.5 million profiles. The analysis focuses on video content and the accompanying auditory signals for signal evaluation. Results indicate that crowd-based signals aligned with funding success across all three environments, though the specific auditory cues showed a stronger correlation with outcomes on more interactive platforms featuring audio. These findings suggest that crowd dynamics are a key determinant of fundraising results, Suggesting these signals are viable for refining existing platform algorithms and informing strategic marketing decisions.

While Machine Learning (ML) excels at identifying network attacks, deploying these models in practical settings necessitates continuous retraining with up-to-date threat data. Organizational reluctance to share sensitive data with external entities, however, hinders the acquisition of diverse training samples. To overcome this barrier, we introduce a Cyber Threat Intelligence Sharing (CTIS) framework designed to facilitate collaborative learning among multiple institutions while rigorously safeguarding data privacy. Specifically under the paradigm of federated learning, this scheme enables the real-time exchange of extracted threat features and their corresponding model parameters, thereby building upon established findings that such an approach yields superior outcome compared to traditional local data silos. Our study further investigates how to effectively share extracted features within the CTIS architecture and rigorously assesses their influence on final model accuracy. Ultimately, we demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves significant advancements in practical settings, as validated by experiments using the NSA Network Anomaly Detection 2.0 dataset with two distinct collaborative sessions.

This paper introduces a novel algorithm grounded in greedy clustering that utilizes post-clustering updates to achieve superior heuristic performance. Initially, these methods generate sequences by minimizing predicted collision durations. Subsequently, they can represent the planned sequences using JSON to evaluate and compare them against competing maneuvers.

Group synchrony describes situations where oscillators organized into distinct clusters converge toward common frequency values within each cluster. This paper utilizes linearized dynamics near equilibrium points to determine sufficient conditions ensuring convergence to such group synchrony. Specifically, we examine toy models consisting of two fully interconnected groups of fully synchronous oscillators; in these setups, differences in initial group parameters cause a persistent, non-zero phase discrepancy at steady state. Our primary findings delineate how initially grouped coupling strength and internal topologies accelerate the convergence process toward the final stable-state separation. Furthermore, we observe that when groups are tightly bound, the transients approaching steady state mirror the transient dynamics of a simplified reduced system. This reduced system links the large-scale oscillatory frequency disparities directly to quantitative group parameter deviations. Finally, we explore how these internal group dynamics and resulting frequency gaps depend on the mode of connection between groups, addressing both fully homogeneous links and those exhibiting spatially structured connectivity.

While Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) deliver superior visual insights for semi-supervised learning in graph-based tasks, their performance is constrained by the high cost of supervised labeling required to scale effectively. Addressing this challenge, this paper presents ISOL (Iterative Sampling with Low overlap to Separate unlabeled from Overlap nodes), an innovative algorithm designed specifically to enhance GNN efficiency with limited labels by integrating pseudo-labeling strategies. Our method iteratively trains a classifier on high-confidence pseudo-labels to identify ambiguous nodes that should be excluded from training datasets. By carefully managing which unlabeled nodes receive pseudo-labels and avoiding nodes with excessive ambiguity ensures more stable model convergence. Extensive testing across diverse real-world datasets highlights superior capabilities of ISOL in classification accuracy compared to existing state-of-the-art solutions for semi-supervised graph tasks.

Accurately identifying objects within video streams is vital for enabling general purpose video understanding. Currently, achieving this requires three-dimensional object templates constructed from both spatial and temporal data to achieve robust accuracy and precision when accounting for objects moving through space. However, creating, matching, and storing these extensive 3D templates place prohibitive demands on memory and computational processing, especially given the complexity and duration of real-world footage. To mitigate these issues, we introduce PatchNet, a novel architecture that decomposes the original 3D template matching challenge into a set of smaller self-similar patch matching sub-tasks. These patches collectively encode comprehensive spatial-temporal context while maintaining compact storage footprints. As demonstrated by our results, PatchNot surpasses existing leading methods in both precision and computational efficiency specifically for detecting vehicles in complex traffic environments, effectively leveraging the inherent regularity found within commonplace visual objects.

This research investigates the universal as well as nearly universal properties of repulsive SU(N) Fermi gases through comparative analysis of quantum Monte Carlo simulations and large-N perturbative quantum Monte Carlo calculations. We demonstrate that while the ratio of the bulk sound speed to the chemical speed, $c_s/\mu$, converges rapidly to its universal limit for small $N$ due to the dominance of repulsive interactions, this rapid convergence does not necessarily extend to other properties such as the compressibility ratio, $\kappa\mu^2$. Additionally, we examine the effects of small density perturbations on energy in systems of $SU(N+1)$ Fermi gases containing an excess particle, revealing that although universal many-body symmetry effects dominate for $N=2$, they are quickly overtaken by non-universal potential details as $N$ grows larger. Finally, the paper concludes that including random contact interactions in these non-universal regimes can effectively average out specific potential details, thereby restoring universal behavior.

This study presents a generalized classical electrical circuit modeling framework for characterizing linear optomechanical systems involving microwave-frequency frequencies. Utilizing circuit components corresponding clearly to optical and mechanical process variables, classical electrical laws are adapted to construct parallel and series resonance models that accurately reflect various known optomechanical setups. Furthermore, the paper establishes conversion processes commonly observed in these systems, calculating key circuit parameters through both methods: derivation from classical equations and extraction from measured electrical circuit analogs. Furthermore, the paper derives critical system metrics, including linear polarization, and power conversion spectra using circuit concepts, demonstrating that the circuit analog approach yields physical insight and a systematic methodology for analyzing specific optical experiments.

Laparoscopic surgery presents a restricted field of vision, and the introduction to image augmentation to facilitate smoke detection for the purpose of alerting the surgical personnel about potential complications has been evaluated. Using first-principles calculations on simple structural models, we explore the origins of the diverse family of perovskite paraelECTrics, specifically focusing on tilting and offset distortions. We demonstrate that minimal configurations composed of just a few octahedra are sufficient to account for these characteristics, although the electronic contributions are negligible and the effects remain entirely rooted in geometry. By minimizing free energy with respect to local degrees of freedom and comparing them to experimental neutron diffraction data, we find a strong agreement. Furthermore, we show that a particular pattern—feature such as the $R5^*$ mode—is crucial for achieving consistency with experimental observations. The study concludes that a global order-parameter approach is insufficient to capture these phenomena, while a recent conceptual framework offering a local picture—similar in structure to our method—is instead validated.

While recent research has explored using Gaussian processes (GP) to model distributions over graphs through "graphical Gaussian processes," our findings suggest this approach can be viewed as a hybrid of graphical Gaussian models (GGM) and FGMs—specifically the later concept applied across entire functions rather than separate nodes. More critically, our analysis of "graphical Gaussian processes" reveals a diagram representing relationships between nodes and edges is subject to duplication due to a symmetric structure; consequently, we advocate replacing it with "undirected hyperfunctional Gaussian models" to offer an interpretation free of redundancy. Ultimately determined through an application using these undirected hyperfunctional Gaussian models on synthetic data alongside real functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) datasets.

Existing quantum processors face limitations due to noise and hardware-specific constraints like limited qubit counts and high gate counts, necessitating the development of classical algorithms to optimize quantum circuit compilations. This study introduces efficient, deterministic approaches to optimize quantum circuits consisting recursively of specific patterns, an optimization process divided into two main steps: determining optimal qubit mappings and deriving optimal instruction sequences. First, we present two optimization algorithms tailored for pattern mapping that achieve optimality while requiring only $O(\log N)$ space; one runs in $O(N \log N)$ time and the other in $O(N \log N)$ time—both improving upon the output of previous optimal methods with a higher space footprint. Following this, we outline two strategies for optimizing instruction sequences, each also producing an optimal result within $O(N \log N)$ space. These methods complete in either $O(N \log N)$ time or $O(N \log N)$ time, respectively, demonstrating that optimizing both circuit mappings and instruction sequences through our proposed algorithms can result in significant efficiency gains across multiple quantum hardware systems.

Average-case analysis serves as a rigorous framework for evaluating learning algorithms, though it relies heavily on specific data and label generation models that often lack statistical realism, particularly regarding the independence of training examples from the underlying ground truth. A predominant approach in this field involves scaling input noise exponentially, yet our research investigates an alternative where inputs are sampled uniformly without exemplifying sampled inputs from sampled data. Surprisingly, within a convex class of functions, this "zero-noise" scenario yields exponentially significant implications. Specifically, we demonstrate that sampling thresholds exponentially dictate both algorithmic running time and sample complexity. Furthermore, we present two compelling practical consequences derived from this phenomenon. Firstly, various noise reduction strategies can be unified under a single theoretical explanation: to achieve statistical efficiency, training data must sufficiently represent the low-noise subsets of inputs. Secondly, our findings reveal an inherent robustness property; effective generalization necessitates that training examples nearly minimize the noise parameter. This suggests algorithms must implicitly identify and prioritize regions where the input nearly minimizes input dimensions.

Advancements in optical techniques now enable investigations into phenomena spanning energy scales from single-quasiparticle excitations to collective collective modes. In this work, we establish that nonresonant spectroscopy allows for the identification of a bi-layer excitonic insulator by examining the collective excitations within an intrinsic electron-hole bilayer system. Our analysis of the observed dispersion characteristics and dependence on final state occupancy supports the conclusion that these modes are effectively described as phonons dressed by plasmons and subsequent screening effects. Additionally, we have performed quantitative simulations using a Bogoliubov-Hartree-Fock framework to illustrate these polaron-related features.

Federated learning enables distributed training of machine learning models by allowing multiple clients to contribute local models without exposing their raw training data, thereby ensuring privacy. However, current implementations face two major hurdles: high communication costs due to frequent interactions, and the disclosure risks associated with model parameters, particularly in data-intensive sectors like healthcare and finance.

The Flatee design incorporates several innovations to make this scalable: first, it limits the frequency of TTEE expansions per client by integrating trained into an efficient and an effective communication protocol. This study demonstrates how to enhance the performance of RE models by integrating trained KGLP sub-models, thereby transferring the learned capabilities of one to the other without requiring additional data synthesis or parameter-adjustable synthetic data. Furthermore, we introduce a new knowledge graph construction framework that dynamically builds an instance database by aggregating existing resources and extracting sentences from papers. Using this derived knowledge graph, we evaluate our model through rigorous tests on RE tasks across three datasets (Clinical, Schema, and Product benchmarks) and on new sentence instances generated by our link prediction algorithm. Our results indicate substantial performance gains across all experiments: our link-informed RE models outperformed strong baselines by ~4-5 percentage points on our synthetic data instances and achieved similar improvements on standard datasets, while simultaneously achieving state-of-the-art results in our novel link prediction system.

This study details the magnetic architecture of Tb3RuO7, a compound featuring alternating-bond RuO2 chains composed of spin-3/2 atoms. Its magnetic topology consists of weakly interacting, ferromagnetic-oriented Ising-type Tb3+ Ising chains (spin 7/2) situated on either side of the RuO2 bands, creating a system modeled as systems of Ising spins subjected to quasi-constant internal magnetic fields. Our findings reveal that the ground-state magnetic structure is not uniquely defined, a characteristic typical of spin systems with long-range internal fields. Instead, a partially ordered (PO) state emerges, where magnetic ordering is interrupted by periodic regions of disorder. We demonstrate that the appearance of this partially ordered state stems from the competition between the internal quasi-dipolar fields and the fluctuating long-range van der Waals dipolar fields. The transition from a partially ordered structure to a partially disordered (PD) structure, observed in a temperature range of approximately 2–4 K, results from the weakening of these internal fields, allowing the weak dipolar interactions to become dominant. The magnetic properties of Tb3RuO7 are comparable to those of Er3RuO7, yet they exhibit a unique transition between partial ordering and partial disordering unmatched by any other system. These findings establish Tb3RuO7 as an unparalleled prototype for theoretical investigations focusing on internal field effects and the states of partial and partial disordering.

Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) are increasingly recognized as effective tools for solving neural science problems, such as encoding sensory data and driving Sensory Motor Integration (SMIs). A critical challenge within these frameworks is ensuring that generated internal representations remain local and structurally robust. This study addresses locality through two avenues: defining it more rigorously and creating representation strategies to achieve it. We begin by establishing formal criteria for locality to derive an optimization objective compatible with standard smooth neural networks. Leveraging this derivation, we introduce Modulated Local Functional Representations (MLFRs)—a technique that periodically repeats spatially localized features across a neural layer using specific activation functions. Experimental results on multiple tasks confirm that MLFR-enhanced MLPs are superior to both standard smooth networks and current local representation methods, demonstrating enhanced efficacy and reliability.

Comprehensive models for probability distributions conditional on features are fundamental to statistical task frameworks such as classification and regression. In practice, however, input covariate distributions frequently shift across diverse operational contexts, leading to performance degradation in adaptive scenarios. Addressing this challenge, we introduce semi-generative models using $P(C=E\mid X)$ to capture the relationship between latent common causes ($C$) and specific observations ($E$). By integrating these models with the Target Encoding technique, we develop a method for covariate-shift adaptation that unifies causal reasoning and the transformation of observed data. Through theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that the resulting transformed labels retain an identical causal structure to the original equivalents. Further assessments using various synthetic setups and real-world datasets confirm the computational feasibility and superior efficacy of our proposed approach.

The theoretical underpinnings for why deep learning performs so effectively across diverse tasks remain obscure from a geometric perspective. This study visualizes deep learning processes through both geometric and algebraic lenses, asserting that its superior performance stems from two key mechanisms: first, extracting inherent data characteristics by utilizing task-specific algorithmic rules within each layer to transform and simplify input representations; second, achieving superior generalization by mapping data into a high-dimensional space—such as via the kernel trick—where spacing uniformity enhances consistency. Experimental results support this theory, demonstrating that utilizing such proposed theories can explicitly improve model generalization performance.

Deforming the integration contours offers a method to alleviate the sign problem encountered by Monte Carlo simulations away from half-filling. However, the resulting Jacobian determinant within the Boltzmann weight limits generic neural network applications, as their floating-point precision cannot effectively handle the associated sparse sign pattern. In this study, we introduce a specialized architecture leveraging tensor products to mitigate both the determinantal Jacobian burden and the associated memory demands. When paired with complex arithmetic, this approach alleviates the sparsity issue and potentially allows Monte Carlo techniques to address broader quantum many-body systems beyond the constraints of the half-filling sign problem.

We examine a composite Higgs framework utilizing the $SU(4)$ extended minimal composite model, where multiple flavor symmetries exist. By implementing complex scalar fields responsible for breaking flavor symmetries, we achieve suppression of flavor-changing neutral currents (FCNC) through minimal extension. Selecting specific vacuum alignment allows us to eliminate tree-level FCNCs, with residual subleading effects suppressed by the scale $\Lambda_f/f$. Furthermore, this setup generates lepton flavor universality violation consistent with experimental observations.

"Virtual-Physical Perceptual Discrepancies" describe stimuli unique to hybrid environments, where generated cues diverge from what users actually experience. This phenomenon stems fundamentally from the misalignment between generated and real-world sensory inputs. Consequently, our understanding and ability to interpret spatial relationships become distorted. Consequently, VR systems offer powerful tools to intentionally modify user perception of space. However, these capabilities also give rise to significant ethical concerns. Ultimately, this paper examines VR-induced perceptual manipulations through an ethical lens.

The research examines how different factors influence language adaptation performance and assesses the tradeoffs between computational resources and anticipated results.

An associative ring $R$ with $\sigma$ elements ($\sigma$ being at most countable) is defined as elementary when it cannot be captured by any proper subset within its Dong topological ring extension, $D(R)$, that remains countable. Countless research has attempted to determine whether all such rings belong to a specific class, or if they fall under the equivalence relation dictated by their boolean-valued extensions, $R^\ast[K][K^2]$. Despite significant research efforts, the question regarding finite rings remains unresolved. In this study, we present a fresh approach to constructing examples using alternative algebra systems. Specifically, we establish a novel infinite collection of $\sigma$-elementary rings governed by alternative systems. Furthermore, under specific conditions, our methods establish the $\sigma$-elementary nature of certain commutative and non-alternative collections.

Social media platforms serve as a primary channel for spreading false rumors, posing significant challenges for various stakeholders. Our research examines the fundamental characteristics of misinformation propagation on Twitter by analyzing over 11 million related use cases involving search terms for misinformation over a period of 11 months. By applying advanced natural language processing models to analyze these searches, we uncover inherent patterns within the queries themselves. Furthermore, we assess the impact of these misinformation searches on user networks through both quantitative network metrics and qualitative analysis of user profiles. The practical applications of these methods, including a proposed technique to detect deceptive search terms, are explored alongside these discoveries.

This study introduces a real-time spatio-temporal event detection system utilizing geosocial media streams. The method determines the distribution of geotagged posts through spatial clustering, while the clustering process itself serves as a feature to identify posts belonging to specific events, allowing for detection without pre-categorized training data. The performance and efficiency of the proposed system are evaluated through comparisons against leading single-stream classifiers, real-time versions of batch-supervised classifiers, and pre-supervised classifiers.

We introduce "FastSkew," an efficient tool for generating skewered realizations of Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) and Large Scale Structure (LSS) fluctuations, specifically designed to accelerate bispectrum-based cross-correlation studies. This tool computes third-order perturbation modes based on the Matter Distribution Simulation Project's (MATS) formalism applicable to general bias functions, while retaining all lower-redshift perturbation terms identical to those in the widely used CMBCode package's INAR method. To match MCMC-based analysis speeds, FastSkew employs a fast Fourier transform (FFT)-based computation approach. When evaluated against third-order Lagrangian bias models, FastSkew produces results indistinguishable from INar within MCMC measurement precision. Consequently, it enables rapid simulation production for efficient analysis of geometric distortions arising from Minkowski metric assumptions applied to an expanding universe. This capability facilitates numerous independent realizations required to quantify statistical uncertainties in proposed CMB and large-scale structure probes for cosmological expansion geometries.

By viewing adversarial training through the lens of Bayesian learning with prior knowledge, this work presents a unified framework that bridges existing approaches. Traditional methods, which limit weight norms to ensure robustness, inspire our proposed prior distribution derived from a quadratic constraint combination. This new prior can be efficiently sampled using spherical decomposition, facilitating robust posterior approximation via evidence lower bound optimization. Furthermore, leveraging KL variational inference with prior samples allows for the integration of existing self-training techniques into this unified perspective, enhancing performance over traditional adversarial training—as demonstrated on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-12 where our method achieves superior results.

Addressing the surge in online rumors on social media platforms became a critical issue during China's COVID-19 pandemic, particularly within the context of extensive government interventions against disinformation. Perceived misinformation can severely damage public health by harming individuals' psychosocial well-being and encouraging unsafe practices. Since social media serve as a primary information channel for seeking health updates, psychological support, and practical guidance, these platforms also foster the rapid propagation of rumors, intensifying public anxiety and undermining adherence to vital preventive measures like social distancing and masking. The paper offers a fresh perspective on rumor propagation by analyzing the structural features of rumor networks within Chinese rumor datasets recorded during the epidemic. The study employs an innovative mechanism explaining how rumors spread and proposes a new computational approach for assessing their specific influence. Remarkably, derived influence values from this approach correlate strongly with observed spreading performance. The findings additionally explore the impact of inherent rumor properties and network topology characteristics on their individual influences. The implications of these insights provide strategic guidance for effective rumor mitigation efforts on the internet.

While a neural network using natural language can serve as a highly effective parser of syntactic structures, existing bounds on its representability do not fully address the layers' architectural designs. We introduce an initial approach to compress such models through quantized weights and addresses the prior lack of quantitative methods by introducing new theoretical bounds on the capacity of deep neural networks used in this context, alongside new techniques for network compression verified by quantitative methods. We demonstrate that only a minimal amount of resources are needed to preserve most of the string-to-string mapping capabilities of the original model.

This study introduces ProCS, a software tool designed to predict high-resolution chemical shifts for protein amide protons (Protein-H^N), based on the specific main side chain conformations. The tool utilizes quantum mechanical methods to predict these shifts, making it the first of its kind to do so for protein amide protons. Experimental data show that the average root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of ProCS-predicted chemical shifts relative to NMR-measured values is less than 30 ppm across three datasets, demonstrating performance that closely matches the results produced by back-calculation methods. Distinguishing from calculation-heavy algorithms, ProCS offers the significant advantage of rapid computation for these high-resolution proton predictions, providing users of chemical shift-based structure validation and analysis with an efficient solution.

The loss function plays a pivotal role in guiding a Deep Learning model toward the correct solution, yet within the realm of supervised learning for pattern recognition—such as image classification—several variations exist. This paper investigates diverse Loss functions by evaluating them on a single classification dataset, CNN architectures are employed for recognition tasks using both natural images (ImageNet 100) and synthetic images (GTSRB). While these approaches employ convolutional architectures to perform the classifications, they employ different variants of loss to optimize the solution space, with final outcomes assessed using accuracy metrics. Although limited variations of losses are examined against just two datasets in this work, it offers foundational knowledge for future investigations into understanding how loss functions influence correct learning across computer vision applications.

Investigating multi-wavefunction duality offers a powerful approach to understanding many-body systems far from equilibrium. In this study, we reveal an innovative link between duality and conserved quantities. We represent two dual many-body states using a single wavefunction situated in an extended Hilbert space; however, the dual consistency condition emerges as a constraint corresponding to a conserved quantity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that duality constraints arising from the Parquet method fit precisely within this framework. By examining specific cases involving attractive Hubbard and $t$-$J$ models in one dimension, we reveal a profound connection between these model dualities and a $U(1)$ symmetry transformation acting on their respective extensions of Hilbert space.

The phase transition from a semimetal to an excitonic insulator arises from the spontaneous opening of an energy gap triggered by the condensation of electronic excitons. Although these excitonic states are anticipated in numerous condensed matter systems, their experimental verification remains scarce. Achieving both observation and identification requires theoretical frameworks that provide comprehensive details on their properties. In this study, we introduce a $\textit{ab initio}$ approach to calculate the critical parameters governing exciton condensation. Specifically, we examine a prominent candidate system, TiSe$_2$. Our results indicate that the critical temperature for exciton condensation in TiSe$_2$ falls within the range of several Kelvin to hundreds of Kelvin. The theoretical framework developed in this work enables the calculation not only of the phase transition temperature but also of emergent phenomena within the excitonic insulator state, including characteristics of superconductivity and photoluminescence.

Recently, U.S. police departments have adopted text-based systems to enhance community safety, enabling citizens to report criminal activities, enable officers to dispatch units, and handle interactions to ensure accountability and protect against accusations of misconduct. While these platforms were designed for general public interaction, including reports from various users, they are also accessible to individuals with ulterior motives, such as malicious actors, law enforcement, or interested parties seeking only to influence outcomes without making real contributions. Consequently, accurately grasping the motivations, behaviors, and goals of different system participants is crucial for effectively managing complex interactions, especially when the system is used to both log incidents and direct police resources. Consequently, this paper introduces a systematic investigation into the complexities of these interactions, leveraging extensive dialogue datasets from a U.S.-based public safety system. Through meticulous data analysis, we identified distinct user profiles, including members of the general public, malicious users, law enforcement, and internal stakeholders, all of whom exhibit varying communication tactics. Furthermore, we uncovered key insights regarding these tactical differences, the structural design of the interface, and the semantic and pragmatic functions embedded within the discourse. To facilitate deeper exploration, we released comprehensive data analysis along with a specialized sub-grammar to pinpoint intricate linguistic and discourse patterns, offering enhanced access to these features. Ultimately, by prioritizing these textual insights, researchers and developers can enhance both system architecture and engagement strategies, leading to more efficient operations, improved user engagement, and heightened overall community security outcomes.

While Prakash's lambda-prolog harmony stands out as the most effective method for merging classical logic with linear logic via dualization—encompassing Prakash's dualizing rules, dualization-based proof search, and the concept of proof nets—it remains largely unfamiliar to classical computability researchers due to its distinctively nonstandard notations. Specifically, these atypical styles present significant barriers, including the difficulty of mastering dualization-based proof strategies and comprehending the structural implications of proof nets. Consequently, this article seeks to clarify these ideas within traditional classical computability frameworks by leveraging dualization-based proof strategies and examining the relationship between harmony and the dual space method within Herbrand's completeness theorem. Through these approaches, we intend to demonstrate how the harmony of classical-computational reasoning functions effectively within this classical context.

While deep reinforcement learning has secured success across numerous domain tasks, deploying these models typically demands substantial human-defined rewards. To address this, researchers have focused on methods that automatically infer rewards from interactions with the pre-existing environment. Despite these advancements, both automatic and manual annotation approaches often consume excessive time. We introduce a straightforward yet time-saving tool designed to facilitate both automatic and human-driven reward creation by pulling on environment visual cues. We call ours "VACR": Visual-Assisted Cluster Ranking. It presents human annotators with multiple system-predicted states and allows them to select the trajectory yielding the best outcome. By leveraging contextual visuals to limit annotation to only a small sample of key checkpoints during training, VACR saves dedicated human effort. Comprehensive evaluations on several robotics benchmarks confirm its efficacy and ability to distill expert knowledge more efficiently than traditional methods.

This work investigates a distinct class of singular vorticity distributions known as pointed vortex loops. Characterized by smooth vorticity energy and maximum circulation that grows without bound as the non-integer power of a small parameter $\epsilon$, these distributions take the form $\epsilon^{-\alpha}p_\epsilon(x)\;a_3$, where $p_\epsilon(x)$ is a smooth, rapidly decaying function bounded by $\sim \exp(-1/\epsilon)$ within a smooth, simply connected domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$. Specifically, $p_\epsilon(x)$ vanishes to high orders on $\overline{\Omega}$ and exhibits a sharp peak near a specific point $x_0 \in \Omega$. As $\epsilon$ approaches zero, these distributions converge to a loop singularity—essentially a smooth curve $\Gamma = \partial \Omega$ supported on $\text{sup } p_\epsilon(x) = \Gamma$, where vorticity is zero everywhere except $\Gamma$. The fluid evolution governed by such initial vorticity converges strongly (in $L^q$ for $q<\infty$) to the motion of thin vortex filaments, subject to the Kelvin inviscid dynamical equations, $\dot{A}_i + \sum_{i<j} A_j \cdot (A_j - A_i) = 0$. We propose AIPWPee—a novel algorithm utilizing neural network estimates for the regression of covariate mu functions and the probability of treatment. Simulations indicate that our method significantly outperforms other techniques regarding mean squared error in treatment effect estimation. This superior performance persists even when our algorithm uses fewer layers or smaller networks compared to competitors, reducing computational costs while maintaining accuracy. Additionally, real-world experiments on three datasets confirm that our method achieves better performance than existing algorithms.

The $\tau$-lepton, as the lepton closest in mass to the scale set by the electroweak vacuum, offers a unique window into both precise electoweak phenomena within the $\tau$-system itself—such as its couplings, decays, and production mechanisms—and fundamental physics phenomena occurring at significantly higher energy regimes. Given contemporary advances in $\pp$ collider experiments, particularly those involving identified forward $\pp$ tagging available at LHCb, ATLAS, and CMS—as well as $e^+e^-$ annihilation studies reaching up to approximately 116~\GeV$$—these investigations have reached a phase of exceptional sensitivity. Consequently, theoretical frameworks are now being challenged by these new empirical insights. This presentation examines critical theoretical challenges required to meet these heightened demands, covering the lepton's couplings and partial or total decays; muon-$\tau$ magnetic coupling; five-body or fewer decays; hadronic coupling; and production mechanisms. Specifically, I will introduce current lattice QCD developments addressing hadronic vacuum polarisation contributions to $\tau$-related processes.

This study utilizes flow within a rotating annulus to examine how numerical models represent physical dynamics of baroclinic waves. The investigation begins with experiments on a two-dimensional annular base state featuring radial salinity or temperature gradients; this setup benchmarks experimental data against the COMSOL multiphysics COMSOL model, which simulates these effects. Once experimental results benchmarked, the same conditions are simulated using the OSU-NCAR baroclinic wave model to evaluate its capability in generating baroclinic waves. Consequently, a comparative analysis concludes that while numerical simulations generally produce dynamics consistent with experiments using comparable initial conditions and parameter values, specific quantitative discrepancies arise due to subtle parameter variations and numerical discretization limitations.

Pruned DTW (PrunedDTW) operates within a specific bound around a specific series thereby allowing it to discard regions of a incoming series that fall outside of Pruning Distance threshold. This paper presents an innovative variant designed to accelerate the comparison of a single reference series against a new input. By leveraging the two-dimensional properties of the search region Pruning distance can be replaced using diagonal calculations thus enabling the series to be abandoned even sooner. Experiments demonstrate this variant achieves speedups of nearly one order of magnitude. Testing plays a vital role in modern software quality assurance, yet writing effective tests remains difficult, leading many industry professionals to rely less on quality assurance outputs due to a lack of confidence in those outputs. Teaching these skills often suffers from traditional approaches grounded in syntax-oriented testing techniques that fail to address the underlying conceptual flaws of poorly designed cases. To mitigate this, researchers introduced an innovative testing curriculum centered on systematic testing strategies to foster deeper conceptual understanding. This study evaluates two feedback mechanisms used during problem-solving exercises within this new curriculum: traditional detailed feedback and an innovative inquiry-based approach designed to prompt students to identify their conceptual gaps independently. Through a large-scale empirical study using a mixed-methods design and data from 190 participants, the study compared the learning efficacy of these feedback methods. While both provided comparable overall learning gains, the detailed feedback proved more efficient for acquisition skills, whereas the inquiry-based approach drove superior acquisition of advanced testing concepts and was preferred more highly by students and instructors alike. Furthermore, qualitative insights gathered from students highlighted perceived barriers related to individual learning preferences regarding the type of feedback received and institutional constraints that constrain teaching methodologies.

Explainable AI has become a vital research area, largely due to advancements in Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) operating within multiple domains. Yet, contemporary standards for explanations fall into a dichotomy: either they provide excessive detail lacking expressiveness by merely analyzing input data, training examples, or intermediate layer activations using unsupervised methods like feature visualization, or they offer too much generality expressiveness while sacrificing specificity because they omit detailed dataset insights into semantic structures. To overcome these limitations, we propose an innovative binary framework capable of generating highly expressive explanations from DNNs. By integrating the analysis of concept sequences—derived from natural language labels for images (e.g., in CIFAR-10) or detected bounding box categories (e.g., in COCO detection tasks)—with the pixel-level analysis of visual inputs, we formulate a Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP) approach. This method elucidates the functional relationships among semantic patterns at a high level and identifies the critical constituent pixels within each concept that drive the network's decision-making. Empirical evaluations across CIFAR-10 and COCO datasets demonstrate that our model produces more meaningful and understandable interpretations of DNN logic compared to existing state-of-the-art models.

This paper investigates inference regarding the stationary mean within a multivariate time series that exhibits heavy tails and lacks stationarity. The James Webb Space Telescope's (JWST) first observations primarily targeted the galaxy-merging lens system, EL Gordo, featuring two Einstein rings, although initial analyses by Grcevich & Kocevics (2019) suggested a quadrupole configuration. Cardiology specialists typically diagnose heart issues by analyzing cardiac cycles within phonocardiograms, making automatic cycle detection vital for telemedicine platforms. While current state-of-the-art methods rely on Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), they often struggle with noisy real-world clinical environments where cycles are obscured by additive noise or distorted by abdominal movements (convolution). Experiments utilizing an anonymous hospital dataset demonstrate that our proposed approach outperforms previous methods, particularly in realistic scenarios involving convolution.

This study represents a pioneering experimental investigation into whether bidders in auctions perceive credible auction rules as logically consistent. Specifically, it examines second-price auctions involving more than one round, a scenario where rules require bidders to declare plans for multiple future auctions beforehand and execute those responses. Using a within-subjects methodology involving 160 participants in 10-person groups over two auctions, along with real monetary incentives, the research found clear evidence that participants do not view the standard rule against collusion as credible; they believe they could outbid themselves in a hypothetical third-price auction to achieve outcomes better than their initial bid would allow. While established theory asserts that rational bidders have no incentive to collude because the rules are self-enforcing, these experiments suggest a widespread belief in rule inconsistency among actual buyers. Consequently, these results indicate that people often fail to distinguish between auctions when they perceive such enforcement gaps, potentially leading to higher collusive risks. Ultimately, buyers appear influenced less by objectively rational auction strategies and more by what they perceive other participants to be doing in similar scenarios under these conditions.

To mitigate this, we introduce AAAQAcad— a novel dataset comprised of pairs of short information-seeking queries and corresponding responses resolved within single research papers across various domains and various levels of formality. Each example is meticulously crafted and meticulously grounded in the full text of one paper alone. Each example is carefully extracted from long free-text and annotated with start and end indices to navigate precise locating in paper. Finally each sample further includes structured extracts and is enriched with various types structured data. Our experiments demonstrate that current answer-based training techniques yield poor performance, suggesting a need approach that integrates both textual context alongside the existing answer-based training. Additionally we showcase various typed data applications demonstrating human labeling and diverse question answering capabilities.

We investigate small perturbations associated with fast neutrino instability within the core regions of detailed 3D core-collapse supernova simulations, comparing them similarly derived perturbations from well-known 1D models known to produce this phenomenon. The examined perturbations span the region of neutrino sphere where they function as transverse oscillations within fluid modes, transitioning outward to behave as longitudinal fluid mode oscillations. Findings show that while the frequency and amplitude of this instability in both simulations align within an order of magnitude, rapid oscillation in both cases leads to significant issues with standard linear stability analysis due to its dependence on transient transverse dynamics. Consequently, a practical approach utilizing small-scale perturbations observed at larger spatial scales was implemented; this yielded reliable estimates of instability parameters that closely match the direct analysis, serving as an effective method for later integration into neutrino transport simulations.

Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a prevalent condition among children, characterized by a lack of objective diagnostic methods. Prior research into regional brain activity at rest using rs-fMRI and machine learning has indicated distinguishable patterns between ADHD patients and healthy controls. Despite these findings, previous studies failed to pinpoint which specific brain regions drive these machine learning classification differences. This study employs Deep Transfer Learning with rs-fMRI to analyze how machine learning distinguishes ADHD patients from normals across the entire brain and specific ROIs. Results indicate that Deep Transfer Learning matches the accuracy of standard Deep Learning on entire-brain rs-fMRI data. Furthermore, the study validates known literature and reveals additional ROIs sensitive to ADHD detection within the context of whole-brain scans.

Quantum interference within non-equilibrium electrochemical contacts significantly influences charge and energy fluxes through nanostructures. This study reveals, via Landauer-based simulations of narrow two-dimensional systems under quantum Hall conditions, that angle-dependent electron scattering at non-ideal electron liquid injections creates charge density variations governed by constructive and destructive interference. These phase fluctuations trigger thermoelectric switching, where power-generating capabilities can switch based on system parameters, alongside the ability to rectify heat flow depending on the same control mechanism. Furthermore, under specific phase conditions, heat rectification occurs, suggesting that regulating electron injection phases via sample geometry or magnetic fields constitutes an effective strategy for managing heat and energy distribution in future quantum thermal devices. Adjusting magnetic fields or geometric parameters to control electron interference thereby enables thermoelectric switching and heat rectification. Specifically, when constructive or destructive interference patterns form due to phase variations in electron injection within Fermi liquids of thermal systems, these processes dictate power generation control and facilitate the rectification of heat flow. To effectively manage heat and energy transfer through quantum structures, precise regulation of electron injection phases via geometric or magnetic field modifications is recommended.

We introduce a new and scalable approach to manage efficient updates within the DNA storage environment, with a specific emphasis on effectively implementing file system hierarchies and minimizing sequencing errors during the synthesis readout process. In this system, files organized into a directory tree are stored collectively using our proposed synthesis-efficient and sequencing-error-tolerant coding framework. During any synthesis readout operation, this code can decode the entire updated file system by DNA-sequencing only a minimal subset of newly synthesized data, rather than requiring the sequencing of every single base pair in the archive on every update. Furthermore, the code enables the extraction and retrieval of any individual file by simply probing the stored pool with that file's specific DNA barcode. We evaluated the system through extensive computer simulations, which demonstrated that, relative to current state-of-the-art methodologies, our solution provides a superior ratio of storage bandwidth to data rate while sustaining an acceptabilityably low error rate.

Nodal lines serve as two-dimensional representations in real space and act as topological defects within representations of symmetry groups like translational momentum. When nodal lines exist in momentum space, they often exhibit non-trivial topological character defined by a line index derived from a winding number calculated through a line polarization metric. These topological features ensure the robustness against perturbations—a rare exception among topological structures given that typical mappable modes in eight-dimensional Hilbert spaces tend to vanish under slight disturbances. This article provides a historical overview of research on momentum-space nodal lines while highlighting their unique properties and recent advancements in realization and theoretical analysis across physics, particularly within photonic systems and other contexts.

Within a spatial network undergoing periodic motion, a localized region oscillating more rapidly than adjacent areas functions as a source for outward-travelling waveforms. These pacemaker-initiated waves propagate at a consistent velocity, a phenomenon frequently employed in theoretical cardiac rhythm models. This study examines the pacemaker's influence on wave propagation velocities using both stochastic and deterministic frameworks. Notably, both models yield comparable results, featuring an expression for wave speed that depends on three key variables: the distance from the boundary to the center of the pacemaker, the amplitude of oscillation within said center, and the local time- and position-dependent timescale. We verify this approximation experimentally using two distinct systems: an electrical ring where capacitances shift non-linearly with movement, and an optical system comprising an optically active liquid influenced by rapid flashes of external light. Observations confirm high consistency between the predicted and measured speeds of wavefronts.

Deep Learning and AI models demand extensive computing resources, particularly graphics processing units (GPUs), making their development financially costly. Consequently, researchers and practitioners frequently rely on cloud infrastructure and SaaS platforms to access necessary performance capabilities, a shift that introduces distinct challenges alongside benefits. While cloud environments provide flexibility and scalability, they also raise critical concerns regarding data security, privacy, and reliance on external providers. This paper offers a comprehensive evaluation of various cloud service providers and Infrastructure-as-Service (IaaS) solutions to support AI development using high-performance computing. It further investigates specific implementation challenges and best practices for managing distributed data storage, cloud data transfer optimizations, and the creation of AI pipelines in the public cloud.

Clinical text serves as a primary repository for patient health data, yet it remains largely untapped. Natural language processing offers a means to harness these documents for extracting valuable insights. This study proposes a semi-self-supervised framework to simultaneously identify disease classifications and necessary textual features to populate ICD codes. By employing a stepwise training strategy, this system improves representational learning while demanding minimal human annotation. Experiments conducted on the ICD-10-Amendment2014 dataset demonstrate significant performance gains: the model reduced ranking errors by over 50% relative to baseline methods and achieved approximately a 10% improvement compared to deep supervised learning approaches designed to predict ICD codes directly. These findings suggest such techniques serve as an efficient avenue for developing semantic understanding models capable of coding ICD diagnoses.

Machine learning algorithms are essential across numerous artificial intelligence applications. Quantum versions of these algorithms offer potential improvements in specific scenarios, although current limitations hinder their practical deployment: theoretical variants rely on esoteric data access schemes, while experimentally relevant algorithms lack sufficient qubit coherence, robustness, and control. This study addresses these issues by implementing and assessing two foundational quantum models—the quantum generative adversarial network and quantum support vector machine—on commercial superconducting hardware. By analyzing limitations related to data loading, we propose enhanced architectures that utilize smaller qubit counts and eliminate data access assumptions. The presented implementations of these improved algorithms are straightforward to integrate into broader quantum machine learning strategies, serving as an exemplary foundation for quantum-enhanced learning algorithms.
