Analysis focused on Pb--Pb ultra-peripheral collisions recorded by the ALICE detector at the LHC, using a center-of-mass energy per nucleon pair of $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.02\ \text{TeV}$ during the 2017 data-taking period.

Recent advancements have enabled Multimodal Models-based (MMM-G) approaches to synthesize content-aware audio guided by images using "listen-to-image" strategies. These systems typically involve two phases: first, learning a joint representation of image-sound correlations via paired datasets in offline settings; second, generating audio responsive to new input images in online applications. While effective for general pairs, this method often fails to produce precise sounds for specific regions or objects of interest, as it relies solely on statistical correlations trained on entire images. Although "focus-guided" techniques were proposed to enhance spatial accuracy, training their intermediate guidance representations remains challenging. This study introduces a new intermediate guidance module compatible with both self-supervised and unsupervised supervision, eliminating the need for annotated training sets and requiring no additional guidance network training. Evaluated across multiple benchmarks using both self-supervised and paired audio-image data, our proposal demonstrates strong cross-supervisory robustness and superior performance against existing state-of-the-art approaches.

Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are highly regarded for modeling sequential data, yet their adoption in real-world applications remains limited due to inherent drawbacks. These include difficulties in training, the requirement for substantial memory, and inefficient processing speeds. These issues largely stem from the vanishing gradient problem and the inherent limitations of existing training methodologies. Although recent advancements have enhanced the performance of deep recurrent structures by introducing global attention and recurrent gates to capture long-range dependencies, these improvements offer no practical guidelines for optimizing the training of such models for specific tasks. Consequently, this research investigates various training strategies across differing data lengths to determine the most effective approaches for specific scenarios. By empirically analyzing the trade-offs between training time, model accuracy, and prediction efficiency for different implementations, this study provides data-driven insights for selecting appropriate training methods and architectural configurations tailored to unique requirements.

Achieving both public health goals and economic stability during a pandemic proves challenging, yet both sectors rely heavily on each other and influence one another reciprocally. Using a stochastic switching system framework combined with a two-regime Markov Switching Arithmetic Average option model, the paper analyzes an exact analytical solution for determining both economic and healthcare optimal strategies during various pandemic phases. Numerical simulations demonstrate the solution's broad applicability across different scenarios, indicating that well-timed interventions effectively minimize harm to both populations and the economy.

Building reliable machine learning (ML) models, even when provided with adequate computational resources and expert knowledge, necessitates access to bug-free datasets. Unfortunately, real-world data is frequently contaminated with defects that significantly impair model accuracy and robustness. While numerous methodologies exist to uncover dataset anomalies, Shapley Important Permutation Feature Selection (SIPPS), or Shaplet, is widely adopted for this purpose. However, existing algorithms primarily evaluate features within isolated models, thereby failing to account for interactions among features, which reduces their efficacy when the training process involves complex pipelines. To address this, we introduce Shaplet applied specifically to multi-stage data cleaning workflows, termed "Shaplet for Data Cleaning" (Shaplet4Clean). Functioning as an explainable AI (XAI) technique, our method is designed to pinpoint the most influential rows of data within such complex pipelines. We further present a comprehensive framework that integrates these identified critical data points with generative adversarial networks (GANs) to systematically debug entire families of sequential end-to-end machine learning pipelines. Empirical results across various datasets and end-to-end processes demonstrate that our approach significantly surpasses comparable baseline solutions, exhibiting greater efficiency in locating data errors and effectively restoring predictive performance.

This study centers on discrete invariants that closely resemble Ltorentzn polynomials, with the primary conceptual link across these disciplines being a space defined by linear matrices.

This work integrates theory and experiments to analyze pressure-induced switching of the anomalous Hall effect (AHE) in the triangular antiferromagnetic semimetal Mn$_3$Sn, a material known for a vast array of exotic phenomena. Under a modest hydrostatic pressure of 0.43 GPa, the low-temperature AHE in Mn$_3$Sn drops by half, while its magnitude responds non-monotonically to further compression. These observations indicate a phase transition to a weakly antiferromagnetic structure featuring alternating out-of-plane spin components. Such findings highlight the critical role of the bysmaroic antiparallel spin configuration in sustaining the AHE within triangular antiferromagnetic systems. Consequently, this study offers essential insights into current theoretical frameworks and opens new avenues for exploring topological and magnetic characteristics in magnetic Weyl semimetals through pressure engineering.

Knowledge graph construction serves as a critical phase in information extraction, with relation extraction (RE) representing an integral sub-task within this process. While traditional RE relies heavily on textual cues and linguistic knowledge, recent interest has shifted toward training neural models using only positive and negative RE pairs, effectively bypassing the need for rule-based annotations. Consequently, these neural approaches have achieved superior performance on multiple benchmark datasets. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of neural-based RE, examining constituent models, architectural designs, and training strategies while outlining future research directions within this domain.

Graph-based models are widely favored for representing complex datasets, yet real-world scenarios often necessitate more sophisticated structures to accurately capture intricate relationships, making hypergraphs the more suitable choice. However, existing hypergraph learning algorithms suffer because mapping data labels onto hyperedges requires precise supervision; since a hyperedge connects multiple nodes, a single label implies a joint annotation for all nodes within it, a level of granularity frequently unavailable in standard datasets. We address this challenge by proposing a technique to re-construct labeled hypergraphs utilizing only mildly labeled alternatives, leveraging hierarchical relations among vertices to infer probable entities and establish effective supervisory signals. Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that our approach successfully learns robust hypergraph representations, resulting in heightened performance for hypergraph classification tasks compared to utilizing weak or no labels.

Clinical radiology reports represent integral components of standard patient documentation yet remain underutilized in fully structured formats for automated analysis because of the immense effort required for report generation and digitization. To leverage existing data effectively, we created DCA-CXR, an enhanced counterpart to the widely adopted CXR dataset. DxCXR aligns every finding in existing CXR X-ray images with corresponding textual descriptions using precise paragraph-level alignment alongside new semantic annotations for medical entities within each paragraph. Validation indicates our semantic tagging outperforms previous methods, and three advanced computational approaches for extraction achieve state-of-the-art performance through this precise alignment capability. Our complete project, including code at https://github.com/raijuly/dca-cxr, remains publicly accessible.

This work introduces a robust metric for characterizing unidirectional emission in microcavity lasers. While Shannon entropy applied to far-field distributions—calculated within polar coordinates to resolve specific directions—initially appeared suitable, our analysis reveals significant limitations when dealing of arbitrary cavity geometries. In response, we propose an alternative based on the concept of geometric visibility. Demonstrated via simulations of arrow-shaped resonators supporting unidirectional lasing, the experiment shows both the proposed method and the initial entropy approach successfully identified the emission orientation for various cavity scales. However, empirical evidence indicates that the emitted power ratio between opposing directions in the laser threshold is more reliably identified using ratios derived from the proposed formula than those using Shannon entropy, thereby enhancing measurement accuracy.

As a potential digital replacement for fiat currency, fewer major cryptocurrencies exhibit significant stability in their fiat pricing compared to potential investment assets. Yet, if cryptocurrencies aim to function as effective store-of-value or means-of-exchange alternatives, such pricing stability ought to persist even when external markets decline. Our study reveals remarkably consistent local price stability for certain cryptocurrencies—even tighter than that seen in traditional bank fiat—across nearly universal testing conditions, regardless of whether stability is measured globally. Consequently, these findings imply specific heterogeneity regarding currency-substitute characteristics within the cryptocurrency domain, but caution against ignoring substantial differences even within categories like medium-of-exchange alternatives.

We address the large time asymptotics of the ergodic probability distribution function for the height profile within the Zakharov-Shabat (KPZ) equation, specifically under weak noise conditions. This investigation builds upon our earlier work, which focused on the ergodynamics in the absence of noise. Compressible electron-scale turbulent fluctuations are a significant unresolved area within plasma physics. Experimental results demonstrate that this method consistently outperforms existing node allocation algorithms in both efficiency and predictive capability. Furthermore, the approach was validated through numerical analyses of two complex geometric setups with intricate boundary conditions: a square chamber featuring rotating walls for a cavitation study and a channel with sinusoidal walls for secondary flow analysis in viscous fluids.

Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs) are capable of achieving exceptional accuracy on numerous standard large-scale image datasets; however, their performance drops significantly when applied to datasets containing orientation labels (either as rotations or flips), particularly given the common absence of such labels during training. Additionally, NCNs include a specialized training methodology tailored for large-scale oriented datasets to maximize operational efficiency. On three benchmarks—ImageNet, Places365, and COCO—our system matches the accuracy of top-tier non-oriented networks while promptly and precisely identifying the direction of an image.

To address this, we present a novel algorithm called iGMPI, which represents the first policy-based iteration method capable of processing Markov decisions with continuous states while exhibiting convergence rates that depend only on local state information to maintain computational feasibility. We validate the efficacy of iGMPI through two distinct applications: first, by employing kernel density estimation to approximate policies and values in a truncated fashion within a finitestate MDP, thereby simulating continuous-state dynamics; second, by directly utilizing in-state representations of affine policies and value functions in an instance of the Averaged Problem. Our experimental outcomes confirm that iGMPI delivers substantial gains in state-level memory efficiency without resulting in any compromise in computational speed.

Computer models are increasingly ubiquitous in modern science and engineering, often replacing costly physical experiments to facilitate better data-driven inferences, model settings, and result forecasts. A fundamental and widely applicable class of problems involves determining the optimal values for model control settings to achieve desired outcomes, a formulation known as model or experimental design optimization. A critical challenge within this domain arises when these models are slow to execute, particularly if they are not only restrictive roughness but also stochastic; this implies that evaluating a single control set requires a separate model run to account for random fluctuations. This document re-examines the optimization of noisy simulations, introducing a method based on a new contour-based approximation. This approach offers a solution suitable for high-dimensional problems where the objective function is both a biased and expensive estimate of an underlying smooth average function of continuous interest functions or time series. Applying this approach to optimizing the outcomes of a volatile time-series-based operational weather model, we demonstrate that our technique significantly outperforms traditional "one-at-a-time" adjustments and standard finite-difference gradients by reducing the number of required function evaluations to locate superior solutions compared to comparable computational costs."

For the first time, the ALICE collaboration reports findings on how complex jets fragment within a medium, using photon-jet correlations as the primary evidence. In this setup, an initial photon acts as the baseline for determining the transverse momentum ($p_{\text{T}}$) of the unobserved initial jet. The analysis compares the yielded particle spectra inside these medium-modulated jets against the same spectra in uncorrelated photon-$\gamma$+jet events, with results normalized to the photon-jet $p_{\text{T}}$ bins. This comparison reveals two distinct trends depending on the initial jet's $p_{\text{T}}$. When the jet's starting $p_{\text{T}}$ is near the medium's saturation scale, normalization shows quenching in high-$p_{\text{T}}$ regions but an apparent enhancement at low $p_{\text{T}}$. Conversely, when the jet's initial $p_{\text{T}}$ is significantly above this saturation scale, only clear suppression is observed. These divergent behaviors suggest that jets with lower initial $p_{\text{T}}$ undergo the most significant medium modifications during the quenching process.

The Fisher-KPP equation, an integral part of biological science, gained significant attention following its analysis by this work. While previous investigations into solving this historic diffusion problem have produced numerous outcomes using numerical methods, variational techniques, and analytical approaches, these solutions remain dependent on initial or boundary conditions. Using an analytical method, this research successfully derives an explicit solution for the full spectrum of Fisher-KPP equations, effectively addressing a long-standing issue in the field.

While recognizing handwritten scripts by their pixel arrangement is conventional, identifying specific handwritten math terms from pressure data collected by writing pens represents an innovative approach. This study introduces an innovative technique for duration alignment during the training of statistical parametric speech synthesis. Traditional duration alignment methods, which usually depend on Gaussian assumptions and back-translation to link duration probabilities between parametric and synthetic sequences in duration regression models, are avoided. Instead, we implement a method that uses the median to map back duration probabilities from a non-parametric standpoint. Because this new approach does not rely on the assumption of Gaussian variance, it more accurately models the often observed asymmetry in duration alignment data.

Occupancy modeling is a fundamental method in occupancy studies used to estimate the probability that a species inhabits a specific site while accounting for imperfect detection. Over time, various approaches have emerged to examine detection processes alongside potential covariates, co-occurrences, and environmental variables. Among these, spatial occupancy models represent a significant development, offering a sophisticated way to understand how the presence of a species varies across the landscape. However, until now, no specialized software existed that could efficiently fit these multi-species and spatial models while properly handling detection uncertainties. Introducing the **spOccupancy** package in R, this new tool fits single-species, multi-species, and integrated spatial occupancy models. The package addresses critical factors, including the counts of observed individuals, the detection of multiple marks per site, spatial relationships, and the inclusion of spatial random effects. These model variations enable researchers to analyze the effects of spatial traits and interactions while correctly adjusting detection errors; furthermore, **spOccupancy** provides functions for model selection and predictive mapping that can be used to predict occupancy likelihood across continuous environmental gradients. Through both simulated and empirical datasets, we evaluated the model's performance and predictive accuracy under diverse conditions. The utility of **spOccupancy** is demonstrated through real-world examples featuring data on the bird species *Parus major*, the freshwater crab *Paratya parva*, and the California spotted owl (*Strabo occidentalis*).

The critical shortage of dermatologists is a pressing global crisis that disproportionately affects low- and middle-income nations, particularly those lacking sufficient clinical personnel to deliver equitable and timely diagnostics for skin lesions. To help bridge this disparity, the Skincare project has been developed as an advanced, cutting-edge computer-aided diagnostic (CAD) tool tailored for skin lesion diagnosis. Utilizing state-of-the-art deep learning algorithms, Skincare empowers healthcare providers to efficiently triage patients, offering immediate recommendations for secondary examinations or treatment while also facilitating effective triage processes. As this system is optimized for mobile deployment, it can be deployed via mobile devices to enhance diagnostic capabilities in regions where doctor availability is scarce. Consequently, Skincare has the potential to dramatically improve access to dermatological care and foster more equitable health outcomes across varied geographical areas. This publication introduces the Skincare CAD system and its associated software architecture while also detailing its evaluation on an extensive, publicly available dataset of moles and birthmarks.

We introduce a probabilistic autoencoder designed to model the evolution of Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) via spectroscopic time-series data. Each data series comprises multiple spectra gathered across various epochs, featuring specific parameters like flux at certain wavelengths and their corresponding measurement uncertainties. Our methodology estimates these latent representations by maximizing the evidence lower bound, utilizing stochastic gradients for optimization. The resulting probabilistic framework explicitly accounts for spectral series characteristics and their associated errors, a critical factor for accurate classification of supernovae, especially given the increasing data volume from projects like the Palomar Transient Survey which continually reduces observational uncertainties. Furthermore, our approach offers substantial flexibility: it can analyze arbitrary spectra and collection strategies without demanding extensive recalibration, and the method extends readily to extended Bayes factor computations for statistical class discrimination among supernovae classes.

While the large-scale dynamics of plumes have been well-established since the early 20th century, the entry of ambient fluid remains a complex area for neutrally buoyant cases and is significantly more challenging when sediment is involved. This study examines this issue within particle-laden turbulent plumes using both $3D$ DNS of rising hot plumes and corresponding laboratory experiments with hydrogen bubbles as a proxy. Measurements from this comparison provide the time-evolving velocity and concentration fields of both the bubble agent and the physical fluid. To evaluate how particles influence entrainment, a bulk model was employed for comparison against outcomes derived from an entrainment closure formulated by Duran-Masdeu et al. (2021), extending their approach to vary with local particle loading. Results show that the direct presence of bubbles alters the relationship between ambient intake velocity and the rising bubble velocity; specifically, as the particle Stokes number ($St$) intensifies, the normalized entrainment rate increases. Consequently, particle-laden plumes draw in more surroundings than their clean counterparts, particularly during the initial phases of their rise.

The propagation of infectious diseases presents a major challenge to global public health, prompting significant theoretical investigation into SIR-type frameworks that categorize individuals into susceptible, infected, and recovered classes. When scrutinizing finite populations, researchers have established that the probability of an outbreak failing to take hold prior to total extinction of the initial infection introduces a spectral limit dependent on the population's interaction structure. Previous studies conducted this analysis solely through adjacency matrices, implicitly treating groups of three or more as symmetrically connected. This study extends SIR dynamics to general hypergraph structures, revealing that neutralization thresholds exhibit nuanced variation based on specific higher-order interaction patterns. We derive lower limits on this extinction probability that converge with simulated outbreak data to an exponential precision. Furthermore, our findings for arbitrary hypergraph topologies are summarized using simplified graph representations; however, these projected thresholds may underestimate true extinction likelihoods, as such projections can fall below the actual threshold values for certain configurations.

We present first-principles-derived spin textures for CrI$_3$ monolayers and bilayers, which feature magnetic moments aligned along the $c$-axis. While the textures of both structures are ferromagnetic, they exhibit markedly distinct characteristics; specifically, the electronic band structure of the bilayer supports the presence of Rashba spin splitting. Notably, the magnetic bond angles within CrI$_3$ bilayers demonstrate sensitivity to strain.

Observations of cool extrasolar stars indicate they possess differential rotation that opposes that of the Sun, a counter-intuitive counter-differential tendency found particularly in sub-solar rotation regimes. Theoretically, convective reversals in convection zones can produce this anti-solar differential behavior. Using direct-current mean-field dynamo models, we examined the influence of this phenomenon on magnetic cycles. By adjusting a free turbulent alpha-coefficient and varying the shear type from solar to anti-solar (supported by 3D simulations), we analyzed magnetic activity in slow-rotating stars. We found that magnetic periods remain stable regardless of the shear direction, yet the magnetic amplitude is sensitive to this differential motion. Notably, adopting real 3D-derived magnetic profiles under conditions of weak rotation can increase amplitude by roughly a factor of 2.5 compared to traditional Mean-Field approximations.

Multimodal deep learning approaches have shown significant success in diverse tasks, yet existing methods often struggle with unbalanced modality inputs and depend heavily on complex, intricate architectures. This paper introduces the **GKFD-Net**, a novel shared-representation k-fan multimodal deep model. It addresses the challenge of harmonizing weights for unbalanced inputs through a simple gradient balancing technique. The architectural design features multiple parallel sub-networks, each processing a specific modality independently before their integrated features guide the final prediction. Additionally, the method employs an Attention mechanism to dynamically focus on critical features within each branch. The proposed technique exhibits excellent flexibility and was extensively validated across six large-scale datasets to evaluate its performance under various scenarios, demonstrating both superior efficacy and structural simplicity compared to current state-of-the-art methods. Experimental results highlight that GKFD-Net achieves comparable or better accuracy while significantly reducing the total number of model parameters and training time relative to existing techniques.

Model checking serves as a prominent technique for verifying multiprocess programs, though fully exploring the state space remains prohibitive for programs featuring extensive threads. To address this, several works have introduced context-aware model checkers designed to selectively branch execution based on specific program properties, with current implementations primarily relying on pre-analysis of static dependencies like memory orders and control structures. In contrast, we present McMini, a model checker that utilizes more general properties derived from actual runtime execution to determine which states require exploration. Its core mechanism employs DPOR (Partial-Order Optimization) tailored to prioritize branch-taking decisions during these analyses. Furthermore, McMini offers versatility through its ability to accommodate various user-defined predicates via an easy integration process. Our results indicate that McMini not only achieves greater flexibility, but also surpasses the efficiency of existing tools.

As the prevalence of online misinformation grows, researchers increasingly investigate its causes and effects. Particular concern exists regarding misinfodemic impacts on healthcare decisions during the COVID-19 pandemic. Since usage statistics indicate that over 60% of pandemic misinformation has originated from WhatsApp challenges have arisen concerning potential solutions targeting this specific platform. This paper offers technical insights into the proposed "Verified Senders Mechanism," designed to label legitimate accounts to distinguish them from unverified users. We analyze the technical feasibility and unintended consequences of implementing message forwarding restrictions within WhatsApp networks. Our findings reveal that blocking forward actions fails significantly due to centralizing technical constraints and significant risk profiles. Technical analysis indicates message limits serve ineffective purposes regarding misinformation prevention due to centralized technical limitations. We estimate that 93% of online misinformation involves shared links rather than individual text exchanges, suggesting that link-based mechanisms might counter these issues effectively. Evidence indicates that 87% of WhatsApp links originate from non-technical sources such as online directories, community forums, and free account sharing sites like Linktree and Lnk.Bio, indicating these sources account for the vast majority of misinformation cases.

This study examines the site frequency spectrum (SFS) arising from coalescent processes linked to a branching process with non-negative (not necessarily finite in expectation) offspring distribution that exhibits a supercritical profile. Assuming a large effective population size $N_e$ and conditions ensuring that $NE_{ne}$ grows to infinity as a subcritical scale parameter $E_{ne}$ approaches infinity, our findings demonstrate that the standard asymptotic approximation of the SFS proposed by Woelfel and Haeseler remains valid. Specifically, while the average extinction rate within such supercritical branching processes is a subcritical value derived from a mean-field approach similar to Laplace transforms used in estimating probabilities of events, our simulations suggest that these processes may not fit certain model assumptions. Although the Woelfel-Haeseler method appears numerically reliable for such supercritical branching populations based on theoretical considerations, it is worth noting from practical simulation results that such supercritical events are rare when considering the expected number of individuals in a sample of size $n$.

The primary goal of spoofing detection systems is to identify synthetic artifacts embedded in speech resulting from synthesis or conversion processes. This paper introduces the novel Intentional Activation Function (iHardAttention), a component tailored specifically for spoofing detection. Grounded in Bayes' Theorem and 0-1 loss to estimate a speaker's intention regarding whether their speech is authentic or synthetic, hHardAttention operates by averaging these intention scores across the entire audio feature sequence while maintaining computational efficiency relative to batch size through constant-time operations. We further propose two derivative functions, SoftHardAttention and DynamicAttention, each balancing expressiveness and computational complexity differently. These functions have been integrated as intermediate modules within neural networks of various architectures used for detection tasks. Evaluations on the ASVspoiv-2019 Parry synthesis track demonstrate that Soft2Harmless is the standout performer, achieving substantial reductions in equal error rates compared to existing state-of-the-art solutions, with additional results presented for other configuration combinations.

Supergravity, a key extension of general relativity, is a compelling candidate for a unified framework and may hold early-universe dynamics within its domain. Consequently, supergravitational EFTs of cosmology represent an underexplored area with significant potential. This work presents a systematic construction of local supersymmetric EFTs involving a single inflaton field and general scalar-tensor dynamics without the single-field constraint, utilizing the supersymmetry non-linear sigma model. By applying this method within both four-real- and four-complex-parameter sectors, we derive two- and three-parameter non-linear sigma models capable of supporting inflation. These models are subsequently mapped into supersymmetric scalar-tensor EFTs of single-field and multi-field scenarios in the scalar potential and kinetic forms, with explicit expressions provided for all parameters including the scalar potential function.

Nonreciprocal optical systems, which exhibit distinct transmission characteristics depending on the direction of propagation, are frequently realized through coupling two ports with a fixed phase offset. Although pair correlations produced in spontaneous four-wave mixing (SPWM) have been utilized for active optics applications, this study reveals an often-overlooked nonreciprocity specific to the correlation phases themselves. We demonstrate that the SPWM-generated correlation phases follow different paths for signal and idler photons; notably, this effect relies solely on the wavevector phase offset shared between modes, in contrast to more intricate requirements necessitated by traditional nonrecipropalities in transmission. Crucially, we establish that these correlation-phase differences at the output can quantify the underlying wavevector phase offset, even in scenarios where photon pair spectra and transmission rates remain fully reciprocal. Experimental results validate this effect, achieving insert efficiencies greater than 90% with an asymmetry index exceeding 9.5. Beyond detection, this SPWM-based mechanism offers versatile utilities, including generating nonreciprocal phase shifts spectral to a broad range of optical elements and implementing isolators in the domain of quantum communications.

Superconducting quantum circuits are among the most promising platforms for building quantum computers, yet deciphering complex quantum phenomena within these systems often demands insight into scales spanning micrometers to nanometers. To address this, we have harnessed near-field scanning optical microscopy (NF-SEM) combined with a plasmonic tip functionalized by a gold nanoparticle to map the terahertz electromagnetic fields arising from two different superconductive quantum loop configurations. Our findings confirm terahertz nanoscaling technology enables the precise visualization of photonic fields within these photonic chip-based superconducting loop resonators. We demonstrate near imaging of photonic THz waves within two different resonant structures.

While it is well-established that the real line can be partitioned into Borel sets of varying orders $\alpha \in [1, \omega_1)$, where each set exists at precisely the cardinality and ordinal stage corresponding to its defined order, providing explicit partitions remains challenging. For instances corresponding to $\alpha = 1$ and $\alpha = 2$, such sets are readily constructible; however, significant difficulty arises for orders greater than these base cases. To address this issue, the work defines explicit functions capable of generating collections of Borel sets for orders $\alpha \in [\,3, \beta) \subset \mathbb{N}$ under specific conditions. Additionally, it addresses the problem within the framework of ZFC and explores the consistency relative to stronger axonomical assumptions.

Financial markets are continuously shifting due to internal factors like policy changes and external pressures such as geopolitical events. Furthermore, the specific paths taken by asset prices rely heavily on nonlinear interactions among numerous investors. Consequently, traditional linear measurement tools often fail to identify how certain strategies generate returns. This research introduces a new approach that determines whether innovations in investor behavior reap past performance gains or only capture future returns once they appear. We test this methodology using an established agent-based simulation (Artificial Stock Market) incorporating financial leverage and historical strategy data from 1986 to 2005. Our simulations reveal that while trading strategies successfully exploited market inefficiencies triggered by the Stock Options Revolution, the returns they previously generated could not be fully replicated by subsequent variations of those same strategies.

Protocol detection involves the critical network security task of identifying properties of received packets to choose suitable inspection protocols, which helps prevent issues like buffer overflows, denial of service, or system hangs caused by malformed or deceptive inputs. While effectively covering all possible malformed inputs is computationally prohibitive in practice given the vast combination counts for each category, existing research addresses risk mitigation through individual, standalone strategies like fuzzing, mutation attacks, and side-stepping instead. This work executes comprehensive empirical studies across representative dynamic protocol analysis tools utilizing these distinct approaches separately. Results indicate that when deployed in isolation, these methods fail to satisfy the protocol detection components of commonly used monitoring software. To execute real-life scenarios effectively, however, a unified attack strategy integrating these various methods is essential.

Electrostatic gating typically controls electron or hole transport in normal metallic states, but under the superconducting proximity effect, it can alternatively modulate the flow of Cooper pair pairs. Our investigation reveals that simultaneous interaction with superconducting materials also allows precise manipulation of magnons—collective magnetic spin excitations—through two distinct gating mechanisms: direct contact and noncontact (proximity) approaches. Specifically, we found that separating a magnetic thin film from the superconducting contact by a dielectric gap of approximately 5 nm effectively suppresses magnon signals. Similarly, varying the carrier density in the metal via an external electric field enables active switching of magnons without physical contact. At room temperature, such proximity-based control offers promising avenues for generating, detecting, and logically processing magnonic waves essential for next-generation spin wave circuitry.

Federated learning serves as an effective strategy for collaborative training across multiple devices while preserving local privacy, but traditional methods struggle when applied to newly introduced data classes. Furthermore, the requirement to gather equivalent data from all participating devices hinders its adoption in real-world scenarios where some users lack representatives for every class. To address these limitations, we introduce an innovative framework designed for federated audio classification that benefits from a zero-shot approach to handle data arising from novel classes. We also present a unified loss function capable of simultaneously performing standard training and zero-shot generalization on a unified dataset. Additionally, we optimize the zero-shot component by employing a contrastive learning technique, thereby enhancing its effectiveness. Finally, we evaluate our methodology against both centralized learning and conventional federated schemes using two comprehensive datasets, Undercommons-EVC and Urban Sound 8K (US8K), demonstrating empirical evidence that suggests our method holds significant potential for broader deployment.

This Letter introduces a theoretical framework designed for comprehensive optical analysis of high-dimensional Greenberger-Horne-Zeinberger (GHZ) resources. The study initially validates this methodology through complete measurements of distinct three-photon GHZ states within a tripartite quantum basis. The approach is subsequently generalized, with a full photonic hyper-entanglement and quantum Fourier transform integration. The utility of this proposal extends towards enhanced multi-photon capabilities for both quantum computing and quantum communications in higher-order dimensions of entanglement.

This study proposes a channel estimation method targeting intelligent reflecting surface (IRS)-aided multi-user multiple-input multiple-output (MISO) systems. Assuming full IRS passivity, reconfiguring the surface multiple times induces multiple cascaded reflections between the UAV and IRS. Treating each iteration as a distinct phase, the approach utilizes the separated channel models established from the preceding stage to facilitate subsequent estimations. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that the suggested algorithm achieves performance comparable to existing methods while significantly reducing computational complexity through the use of diagonal approximation, thereby enhancing estimation efficiency with higher savings in processing demands relative to alternatives.

We analyze American local newspaper coverage surrounding COVID-19 utilizing an extensive dataset of nearly 11 million online articles. By linking newspaper and county-level metrics such as cases, deaths, and audience size, we examine relationships between news production metrics and consumption across time and geography, avoiding reliance on archival files of missing print editions. Findings indicate that consideration of fear appears inconsistent; instead, coverage volume seems unrelated to fear-provoking statistics like COVID-19 severity while remaining independent of actual audience levels. We observe a positive link between coverage intensity and newspaper subscriptions within counties experiencing rising infection rates. Conversely, subscription numbers remain uncorrelated with reported death rates yet show increased growth alongside surges in cases. These results provide implications addressing both the patterns of COVID news creation and the dynamics of public engagement with media coverage.

Counting is an essential human ability often described as an "evolutionary mismatch," meaning it is a useful contemporary capability that could not arise solely through individual learning. We investigate this acquired skill using recurrent neural networks, which begin limited access to stored knowledge about an item's prior frequency. Initially, these models treat each input as independent, but once they are permitted to recall an entity's previous occurrences, they automatically develop a biased expectation for that entity during prediction tasks. We apply this mechanism to a basic 1D permutationally invariant environment where specific rules govern whether an entity appears one or two times per instance. We observe that these models acquire this contextual bias and subsequently optimize their performance according to the predominant pattern in their training data, effectively generalizing to longer sequences of repeated items. Furthermore, we utilize a uniformly mixed distribution scenario to empirically validate their capacity to generalize to novel, unseen sequences rather than merely memorizing. We conclude that such systems with access to memory exhibit behavior functionally comparable to an observer with "prior expectations," thereby producing predictive distributions that align more closely with rare or common patterns rather than assuming independence at each step.

Bloom filters efficiently manage fast, approximate membership checks within minimal memory, making them ideal for enabling quick "mismisses" during lookups in systems ranging from databases and networks to caches. Historically considered optimal general-purpose filters due to space and time efficiency on massive datasets, their utility was lately challenged by Cuckoo filters—which offer exact membership verification—and set-on-hash-trees, a technique allowing both precise individual lookups filter-while maintaining ordered retrieval capabilities.

We introduce Xor filters as a novel approach that combines the strengths of Bloom and Cuckoo filters with unique advantages. Specifically, Xor filters deliver accurate (certain) membership testing in both directions, support efficient updates, and allow for compact data packing through set-oriented operations. Furthermore, they enable deterministic worst-case performance guarantees. We establish theoretical bounds defining the limits for constant amortized update times and worst-case time complexity for operations across the general family of Cuckoo filters. Our analysis demonstrates theoretically, with practical validations through experiments, that Xor filters achieve smaller footprints than Bloom filters while maintaining comparable operational speeds, and that they surpass state-of-the-art filter performance when handling general approximate membership.

This study details three empirical approaches used to assess the predictive capability regarding future market returns of the directional information inferred from the chronological sequence of time-stamped trades—each defined by their execution price and volume. These methodologies examine how the required function maps the ordered set of order execution details onto finite-dimensional spaces through specific functional representations. Applied to historical limit-order book data from the E-mini S&P & S&P Financial Sector indices on CME, the analysis confirms that sequential information derived from trades consistently forecasts returns, often matching or exceeding the predictive power of standard volume metrics. Most significantly, these methods enable constructing backtestable portfolios that generate superior performance relative to strategies relying solely on trade volume.

This study explores robust federated learning (FL) under horizontal partitioning, where FL clients may act maliciously by sending distorted model updates via biased gradient scaling, outlier vector magnitudes, or selective data dropping. To counter these attacks, the authors propose FLVoogd, a novel approach that integrates the generalized Bayesian shrinkage prior with personalized federated learning. By individually smoothing each client's data examples, gradient vectors, and online model parameters according to this prior, FLVoogd achieves invariant estimation regardless of specific bias scaling, outlier outlier sizes, or dropout frequencies. The mechanism reduces both the scale and dispersion of client contributions through variance stabilization before aggregation. Furthermore, by leveraging client-local validation datasets for expected value estimation, FLVoogd enables end-to-end pre-deployment deployment on practical hardware such as mobile devices and microcontrollers without compromising privacy, as no sensitive gradient or parameter data is transmitted to the server. Empirical evaluations across image classification and regression tasks on diverse FL setups demonstrate that FLVoogd significantly outperforms existing robust methods in real-world FL environments on mobile and IoT devices.

While driving simulations provide an excellent foundation for training deep learning models due to their ability to generate abundant, annotated data, deploying these algorithms in the real world often encounters a Sim2gap challenge. This discrepancy arises from visual differences between simulated and actual environments. To mitigate this challenge, we introduce a training strategy where we modify real images by applying simulated variations of depth and camera movements to them. This approach substantially lowers the domain gap by reducing the visual divergence between training data and actual operating conditions. We evaluate this method across two contexts: first, varying real lighting simulations alongside the second, simulating different operational sensor movements on top of the real light variations. In both cases, our technique consistently outperforms baseline models trained exclusively on synthetic datasets. Additionally, this methodology demonstrates robust generalization when tested on data collected from distinct driving environments not seen during training.

The discovery and subsequent characterization of an atmosphere on a temperate sub-Neptune via the detailed study of its transiting signal would be a major milestone. While the equilibrium thermodynamics of transient events typically favor the stable molecular forms of gases, the actual chemical equilibrium of the atmosphere may heavily favor molecules like CO, NH$_3$, and H$_2$O, a distinction driven by kinetic barriers and transit dynamics that can create apparent contradictions. This discord can mimic a condensed ocean hidden beneath the signal, shrouding the true underlying chemistry. We introduce the parameter $\chi$, defined as the ratio of a species' self-van der Waals cooling rate to its radiative cooling rate, to forecast whether the atmospheric composition will align with kinetic translucidity or equilibrium behavior. For the specific case of H$_2$O on a temperate sub-Neptune transiting its star, we find that the lower and mid-atmosphere will show signs of a water vapor supersaturation relative to equilibrium values, a signature that creates transit data resembling a cloudy ocean. Conversely, H$_2$O will exist in its equilibrium state as a liquid within the upper atmosphere layers of such a planet. These dynamics can drastically alter the interpretation of future atmospheric detection results for newly discovered temperate transiting planets, particularly the sub-Neptune class, as the dominant chemical speciation will pivot according to the planet's equilibrium temperature.

Experiments were conducted using the ERB-filtered Marsiyas dataset, which consists of 10 hours of speech from 100 speakers across 100 classes; the system achieved an overall classification accuracy of 80.4%.

The need to monitor industrial systems is widespread, particularly in scenarios involving extensive and variable process categories. This article addresses the specific challenge of real-time change detection and isolation within processes that only provide a limited subset of total available classes. Our proposed framework employs an adaptive strategy combining change detection algorithms with unique isolation techniques capable of managing dependencies among variables. Dependability in these systems is achieved through a structural model representing typical operational patterns. When specific classes exhibit deviations from these baseline states, our methodology detects and isolates them using this structural context alongside a specialized statistical approach built for multi-class identification. The effectiveness of the presented method is confirmed through rigorous analysis and validation via simulation studies focused on pharmaceutical fermentation processes.

We investigate the stellar ages, iron abundances, and alpha-iron ratios in globular cluster systems surrounding dwarf galaxies, utilizing age-metallicity distribution functions (A-MDFs) derived from deep *Keck* spectroscopy of ~100 individual stars per galaxy observed at ~10 Ångströms resolution. By comparing these observations to $\Lambda$CDM simulations, we find that while the mean iron richness and age-biased large dwarf galaxies ($\sim 10^9 M_\odot$) align with simulated predictions consistent with significant progeny inclusion, the smaller dwarf galaxies diverge: their observed alpha-iron ratios exceed simulated values, indicating the simulations overproduce iron relative to other elements (per age) or overrepresent ancient, high-alpha stars within dwarf systems. Consequently, the data suggest that only ancient, chemically distinct dwarf galaxies are captured by the particle simulations, whereas large dwarf galaxies likely contain both early high-alpha populations incorporated in simulations and a broader, iron-enriched star formation history. Regarding the Age-Metallicity Relations themselves, simulations fail to replicate the observed trends in alpha-element abundances across metallicities for Milky-Wave-like galaxies, particularly in lower-metallicity regimes. Finally, we explore connections between our findings and recent claims linking the star formation efficiencies of dwarf galaxies to their initial mass.

Building accurate automatic extraction models for visual-heavy documents, such as invoices, is essential for the widespread adoption of computer vision in real-world applications. However, developing these specialized models typically requires vast amounts of costly human-labeled training data. To address this barrier, this study explores enhancing existing sample-efficient techniques by integrating data synthesized through state-of-the-art semantic segmentation. We focus on extraction tasks for complex, visual-oriented documents within the industry-standard Data 9699 domain. Experiments show that training with synthesized data alone surpasses the performance of previously state-of-the-art models that relied solely on sample-efficient data. Significantly, introducing this synthesized data to an efficient large-language model framework reduced labeling requirements by 90% with negligible impact on accuracy. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that leveraging synthesized data yields logical and systematic performance gains.

By analyzing the results, we identify that interfaces with both antiparallel and parallel large electron spin orientations in EuS and InAs exhibit significant spin polarization at the boundary due to the alignment of In and As atomic positions with the Eu and S bulk planes. Conversely, at an antiparallel orientation between thermal expansion vectors in EuS and InAs, no discernible spin polarization emerges at the interface. These insights aid in understanding and refining the design of spin-polarized interfaces within S+/Magnetic [11] memory architectures.

Although model pruning and acceleration strategies promise to resolve these hardware limitations, existing methods are typically generic, failing to precisely match the computational resources required by specific applications. Designed for practical deployment, our approach allows for the adaptation of pruning granularity based on the specific constraints of target devices. We offer a detailed analysis of how varying levels of fine-grained pruning impact model accuracy and training dynamics across diverse architectures and identify the optimal settings for each workload. Furthermore, we develop trained models tailored to several distinct devices, allowing the selection of models that best fit particular hardware requirements. Empirical results across seven diverse datasets and eight prominent architectures demonstrate that our pruning strategy significantly reduces computational costs while maintaining high model performance.

The identification of gravitational waves generated by neutron star-black hole (NS-BH) merger events is expected to grow significantly following the enhanced capabilities anticipated from the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LIGO-VK) detector network specifically upgrades to their instruments. Classically, these signals are extracted from detector outputs using Bayesian inference applied in the context of gravitational wave observations. Our approach is tested using simulated data from an NS-BH population modeled after the parameter distributions proposed by Behram et al. for the LIGO-VK Observatory during its second observing run. The results demonstrate a highly accurate performance with near-perfect detection and classification rates. Furthermore, we evaluate the generalization ability of our model by utilizing data from an entirely independent population of NS-BH mergers. This new dataset was also constructed through Bayesian inference to determine parameter ranges consistent with waveform features observed in LIGO-VK. We confirm that outcomes on this distinct dataset are similarly excellent, indicating strong adaptability of our model to varied signal characteristics and parameters.

Using simulations to examine how the epidemic threshold responds to diverse network topologies, this study investigates similar limits within the contact process across varying architectures. The research focuses on the theoretical framework linking mean field predictions to phase transitions under random, scale-free, small-world, and assortative community structures, finding a consistent pattern of continuous transitions in all cases. By focusing on long-term behavior where the order parameter signifies the difference between non-existent and established epidemic equilibrium states, the authors observe a distinct rank-based dependency of susceptibility exponent (\gamma') on network degree: as the degree increases, a more pronounced peak emerges in the incidence curve during early outbreak stages. Furthermore, a more extensive and sustained outbreak occurs in networks with lower degree values, indicating higher degree leads to greater degree of infection spread overall.

Actor-Critic (AC) reinforcement learning has become a standard deep RL framework because it combines the sample efficiency of advantages derived under the policy with the ability to explore via its policy. While there are theoretical arguments suggesting that adjusting the exploration-exploitation balance by making the policy stochastic enhances sample efficiency, current heuristics for controlling policy randomness remain inconclusive. This paper introduces a new approach to improving the efficiency of stochastic policy networks by integrating the Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) algorithm into the AC framework. By leveraging the inherent properties of Hamiltonian dynamics, our proposed Hamiltonian-accelerated structure refines action sampling within the policy network and significantly boosts sample efficiency. Empirical evaluations on the CartPole and Acrobatics tasks from the Gym suite demonstrate that this method enhances the sample effectiveness of stochastic policies.

Presence-absence data, where variables are restricted to "present" or "absent" categories, is ubiquitous across numerous fields such as ecology, medicine, and food science. For instance, an ecological context might record the "presence" of various animal or plant species within a specific area, while a medical context might note which symptoms are "present" or "absent" in a patient. This study evaluates various clustering approaches—including "k-Nearest Neighbors" (kNN)-based methods, "Principal Component Analysis" (PCA), and "Hierarchical Clustering"—for this specific data type, highlighting the underexplored difficulty of applying distance metrics that function effectively on binary matrices. To handle this constraint, matrix transformation techniques were employed to adapt widely successful clustering algorithms. Across multiple simulated environments, "kNN"-based methods proved to be particularly robust. Furthermore, applying these "kNN"-based methods in conjunction with an objective function provided a practical method for estimating the optimal number of clusters.

Recent years have seen significant advancements in algorithms for salient object detection, yet current approaches remain largely specific, yielding optimal results only on certain types of imagery such as RGB, R-G-D, marine environments, or medical data. While a universal structure capable of processing multiple modalities like RGB and RGB-D already exists, it fails to converge on state-of-the-art performance across all major modalities. Addressing this gap, this paper presents two enhancements: first, a refined, more robust unified architecture capable of achieving state-of-the-art or near-top-tier performance on R-G-D, marine, and medical tasks while maintaining leading levels of accuracy on input R-G-D images; utilizing this enhanced framework as our foundation, we subsequently develop two novel components—a multi-scale feature extraction module specialized for detecting image boundaries regardless of modality or content type—and a multi-mode attention mechanism designed to leverage both color and depth information effectively in R-G-D scenarios but also handle monoscopic images by operating independently on depth channels where necessary. Experimental validation confirms these proposals significantly contribute to overall model superiority

This study outlines the UM-IU@LING entry for SemEval-2019's Offensiveness Detection Challenge. We developed a hybrid framework combining three distinct submodels to tackle the task. All three were task-specific neural architectures built upon the multilingual BERT framework: the first two handled textual classification for general offense identification across general purpose (Offensive) and non-offensive sub-tasks respectively, integrating offenesiveness indicators with semantic context, while addressing code-switched or non-English slang in social media. Outputs from the separate models were fused using heuristic logic; one subset involved a class-specific threshold strategy, and another employed voting mechanisms to finalize predictions. Notably, leveraging our specialized submodels, we achieved the highest performance among all submissions, securing the Gold Prize (Gold medal position) in this offenesiveness task.

Computed Tomography (CT) is a highly effective medical imaging technique that supports accurate diagnostics, treatments, and analyses by providing three-dimensional anatomical visualization. However, standard CT protocols suffer from high radiation exposure levels and artifacts generated during low-dose acquisitions. Simultaneously, Dual-Energy CT represents an emerging multi-energy technology capable of identifying specific materials within the body, which facilitates targeted treatments and diagnostics. This paper introduces a new reconstruction framework designed to simultaneously mitigate radiation exposure through dual-energy acquisition, enhance scanning resolution by combining data from detectors with varying pixel sizes, and perform quantitative material decomposition. Accompanied by a corresponding mathematical model and an associated numerical algorithm, this model was tested using synthetic phantoms and clinical datasets to validate its efficacy.

Off-line Chinese Handwritten Character Recognition (HHCRC) faces substantial obstacles due to the complexity of Chinese characters and handwritten inputs, especially in low-resource settings involving limited, sparsely labeled data that hinders effective training. To address this, this paper introduces \textcolor[RGB]{red}\textbf{One-Shot CHTR,} an architecture leveraging one-shot learning to create synthetic training data completions. By generating mid-missing Chinese HHCRC images with meaningful context, this framework enhances traditional one-shot methods. Assessments using a selection of sparse-labeled HHCRC datasets indicate that our approach surpasses baseline performance in both accuracy and APER scores. Additionally, we release the source code and intermediate dependencies as intermediate libraries to support future research in Chinese HHCRC.

This work examines how varying levels of correlation influence properties related to heavy nuclei within shell-model calculations. Properties analyzed include binding energies, radii, and root-mean-square root-mean-square distances, all calculated using different cutoffs in the valence-space many-body perturbation theory approach. Specifically, we applied three distinct strategies for handling operator correlations during perturbation theory to ensure convergence of calculated matrix elements. These converged properties serve as inputs for heavy-nuclei shell-model simulations using a fully non-partial-wave expanded no-energy-cutoff Hamiltonian derived via Chiral Effective Field Theory (EFT). Our findings establish binding energies with sub-MeV accuracy and reduce uncertainties regarding correlation effects for nuclear radii from approximately 10% to roughly 5%. Consequently, these reduced uncertainties significantly impact efforts to model unstable nuclei.

Object-oriented programming (OOP) remains a widely used paradigm for developing applications that can run effectively on Graphics Processing Units (GPUs). Nevertheless, GPGPU-based OOP frameworks often result in inefficient memory management and poor utilization of the massive, high-throughput memory available on these devices. Existing allocators are limited by their reliance on sequential memory allocation and free lists, causing memory fragmentation and forcing linear searches during the assignment of memory blocks. To overcome these drawbacks of current solutions, we present DynaSOAr, a parallel memory allocator built specifically around skewed object arrays. Benchmark results indicate that DynaSOAr surpasses existing allocators in both allocation throughput and spatial efficiency while delivering enhanced pointer arithmetic performance.

We demonstrate an atomic impurity undergoing oscillations when accelerated through a spin-orbit coupled Bose-Einstein condensator in the supersolid phase, a mechanism rooted in a distortion of the supersolid's phase during motion. Within a generalized quadrangle $\varOmega$, a code $C$ resides in the Johnson scheme if it comprises a collection $\mathcal C$ of pairwise disjoint cliques from the Johnson graph, where each clique represents a clique of $\varOmega$. Such a code is termed *partial spread* if every point of $\varOmega$ either belongs to a clique of $\mathcal C$ or is adjacent to a point from a clique of $\mathcal C$. Furthermore, this spread is called *neighbour-transitive* if the stabilizer in $\text{Aut}(\varOmega)$ of any clique in $\mathcal C$ acts transitively on the adjacent points of that clique. In prior work, we demonstrated that for any neighbor-transitive spread $C$, its Johnson graph exhibits an adjacent eigenvalue associated with its adjacency matrix, with the associated vector representing an adjacency relationship. Conversely, given adjacent vectors representing an adjacent relationship for every clique in a spread that satisfies these conditions, it can be shown that the spread must in fact be neighbor-transitive. This establishes a robust criterion for verifying the neighbor-transitivity of a given code. Furthermore, utilizing this framework, we confirm the neighbor-transitivity of several previously only vertex-transitive codes found within the $Q(4,q)$ structure.

The Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) represents our Galaxy's most crowded dust- and gas-rich area. Although numerous studies have examined its physical characteristics, its global large-scale architecture remains poorly understood. To address this, we employ a approach derived from statistical physics to analyze CMZ's large-scale density map, utilizing a sample of 139 millimeter-wave sources to estimate dust emission from beyond the galactic plane. Findings indicate that while the scale-free nature often seen in turbulent media persists in both radial and vertical directions, a characteristic scale emerges at large vertical heights (>~100 pc). Additionally, the density map exhibits significant anisotropy; specifically, correlations at fixed intensity are much stronger along the major and minor axes than they are vertically. Comparisons with synthetic maps generated from magneto-hydrodynamic simulations reveal that an anisotropy source similar to real CMZ data occurs only when magnetic fields are aligned with the galactic disk, suggesting magnetic fields play a critical role in CMZ's structural formation.

When a material is exposed to intense femtosecond X-ray pulses, it causes rapid electronic excitations that subsequently drive changes in ionic motions and bond forces. We present new experimental data regarding time-integrated K-edge absorptions within a gold cluster following irradiation by high-fluence laser radiation, alongside a comprehensive rate equation model designed to simulate both electronic and thermal evolution over ultra-short timescales. Our findings agree closely with available measurements and offers robust support for using non-linear time-integrated spectroscopy combined with sequential time rates as a potent method for elucidating ultrafast thermal and electronic cooling processes.

This research investigates the online Euclidean spanners problem, where an online algorithm must maintain a spanner for points arriving sequentially in a complete metric space. Unlike standard online maintenance in low-dimensional grids, our setting assumes no bounded dimension, focusing purely on geometric properties. We introduce a universal constant $s \approx 1.983$ such that any $s$-approximating structure maintained by our algorithm serves as an $f$-approximation for the optimal $s$-approximation of the current point set, with approximation factor $f$ relative to that optimal structure. Additionally, we present a near-optimal algorithm designed specifically for $s = 2$ (i.e., doubling metrics).

Classifying IoT traffic into specific devices or applications is essential for uncovering network vulnerabilities and addressing security concerns that may not be evident through standard monitoring tools to protect private data. While machine learning models have successfully detected these patterns, a critical limitation is their inability to account for features consumed by commercial IoT sensors and controllers, which are both quantifiable and set by clients using pricing models. Since these features are costly in a competitive marketplace, we advocate integrating cost effectiveness into traffic classification algorithms to reflect market value and enhance the system's broader applicability. Addressing this gap, we propose an innovative framework that incorporates feature pricing into both the feature selection training phase and the inference phase of classification.

G\"odel modal logics constitute natural extensions of intuitionistic modal logic obtained via the J\"o nsson-T\"otsuka axiom. They have gained prominence due to their role in investigating GLH, a variant Hila P\"otsky's Hilbert's decision problem, though remaining undecidable. To facilitate computational approximations of this system, we adapt algebraic and relational semantics derived from Lev\"{i}-B\"otsury's work on intuitionistic modal logic. Since these constructions are highly algebraic in nature, we detail two specific semantic frameworks used alternative approaches. First, we identify specific conditions on P\"otsky algebras that characterize G\"odel algebras, with an emphasis on the Jonsson-T\"otsury condition. We demonstrate the duality between the relevant algebras and the corresponding frames, subsequently establishing this result for the extension involving the Lev\"{i}-B\"otsury axiom. Along the way, we provide examples of a nature of alternative G\"odel algebras and frames.

We demonstrate how to align words during live translation by integrating established word alignment datasets. Both approaches perform real-time word dictionary expansion by leveraging the word dictionary obtained from other sources such as parallel corpora or large monolingual dictionaries, thereby enhancing overall translation accuracy.

Standard imaging techniques rely on photons being both absorbed by a detector and subsequently measured; any photon failure to be detected implies no corresponding data point was recorded. However, under specific conditions, photons whose presence at a detector remains unconfirmed can still generate detection data. This work theorizes and demonstrates using full quantum simulations that individuals without absorption even at a sensor can still produce an image. We propose these results as a foundational step toward realizing interaction-free quantum imaging.

The rheology of complex liquids is highly sensitive to interfacial properties; consequently, altering surface properties can produce substantial changes in flow behavior. This fluid-mechanics effect is exploited as a strategy to control movements of objects immersed within such a medium. We demonstrate that passive objects moving through a foam—a representative example of a complex liquid—can initiate active flow patterns. This phenomenon arises because the object's surface roughness generates localized regions of divergent surface tension, creating effective stress forces similar to those in active matter systems.
